q: A team's architecture document is a single diagram of its internal services and their calls. A reviewer says it is not yet an architecture description. Do you agree?
a: Agree. Architecture covers components and their relationships to each other **and to the environment**, plus the principles that guide design and evolution. The diagram shows no external users or systems and no principles telling future teams how the system may change. Add a context view and the guiding principles and decisions; the component diagram stays as one part.

q: A bank's new architect wants the event-streaming platform she used at her last job. The bank is heavily regulated and its operations team knows only relational databases. Which influences on the architecture conflict, and how should she proceed?
a: The architect's own experience is pulling against the organisation (regulation, team skills) and the technical environment. Her preference alone is not a justification, because architecture is shaped by all four influences: stakeholders, organisation, architect's experience and technical environment. She should show which requirements the platform meets better and what the training and operating cost would be. If no quality requirement needs it, the familiar option is the safer choice.

q: A project manager wants to skip the architecture review to save two weeks because the design 'looks fine'. Argue for or against.
a: Against skipping it, though the review can be scaled down. In the lecture's survey, the top reported benefit of reviews was early risk identification (88%), followed by quality assessment and avoiding costly design problems. Reviews also surface requirement conflicts and capture rationale while changes are still cheap. If the system closely repeats a proven design, a lighter review focused on the new parts may be enough.

q: Your claims-processing solution would benefit from a document database, but the enterprise architecture's technology standards approve only two relational databases. What do you do as solution architect?
a: Work within the EA guidance by default, because EA constrains solution architecture. If a specific requirement really cannot be met with the approved options, make the case to the enterprise architect with that evidence rather than diverging quietly. The trade-off is landscape-wide: every exception adds technology variety that the enterprise must support.

q: A document titled 'Solution Architecture' lists class names, method signatures and the ORM library to use. What is it really, and what is missing?
a: It is detailed design: implementable detail plus the choice of implementation tools. Solution architecture should first show, at a logical level, how components work together to meet the business requirements and expected qualities, within the EA's standards and patterns. Without that, nobody can check whether the classes add up to a solution that meets the quality targets.

q: A 'CustomerUtils' module does address formatting, credit scoring and email sending, and five other modules call it directly. Assess it and propose a change.
a: It has low cohesion (unrelated jobs in one place) and high coupling (many modules depend on it), so a change to credit scoring can break the email callers. Split it into cohesive components, each behind an interface that hides its detail (encapsulation). The cost is more components and interfaces to manage, which pays off only if these parts change independently.

q: Halfway through construction the lead architect is moved to another project, yet the team keeps evolving the design confidently. What does this say about the architect?
a: It is a sign of a good architect: one who is dispensable. They documented a viable architecture and shared enough knowledge for the team to proceed without them. Compare an architect who leaves before the team understands the design: that is the 'disappears during construction' failure, and the team stalls or erodes the design.

q: An architect delivers an elegant event-driven design. The team has no messaging experience and the budget allows one operations engineer. Critique it.
a: The design fails on viability: the architect is responsible for a solution that can be implemented **and operated**, and this one exceeds the skill and cost constraints. Re-evaluate the feasible options against those constraints and pick the best one that fits, or include training and support costs in the plan. A simpler design may give up some scalability, so state that trade-off to the stakeholders.

q: To hit a deadline, the project manager wants to drop the security design work. How should the architect respond?
a: The architect supports the project manager on delivery but is responsible for building security, reliability and maintainability into the solution. Make the risk and its later cost visible, then offer a scaled option such as covering only the highest-risk flows now. Quietly accepting the cut would trade a schedule gain for an unviable solution.

q: A ticketing team encrypts every database column. Checkout response time rises from 1.2 s to 2.8 s against a 2 s target. What kind of quality relationship is this, and how would you resolve it?
a: It is an inverse relationship: security (confidentiality) against performance efficiency (time behaviour), for this design and workload. Rank the competing scenarios in the utility tree, then target the measure: encrypt the sensitive fields rather than everything, and remeasure against the 2 s target. The relationship depends on the design, so a narrower security measure may satisfy both.

q: Two utility-tree leaves: (a) 'catalogue page loads in under 2 s with 500 users', ranked (H,L); (b) 'if the payment provider fails, switch to the backup provider within 30 s', ranked (H,H). You have time to prototype one. Which, and why?
a: Prototype (b). Both are important, but (b) is also high-risk to achieve, so it needs the most architectural attention and evidence. (a) is important but low-risk and can probably be met with known techniques. If load testing later shows (a) is harder than assumed, its rank should change.

q: A stakeholder writes 'the system must be highly available'. Turn it into a utility-tree leaf and explain what that gains.
a: For example: 'When site 1 loses power during business hours, traffic is redirected to site 2 within 3 seconds and no confirmed bookings are lost.' Now the requirement is measurable, can be ranked by (importance, risk) and can be checked against the architecture. As a slogan, any design could claim to meet it.

q: After a disk failure, an order system kept taking orders from a mirrored disk. A later power cut lost the last 10 minutes of orders, and recovery took 2 hours. Which reliability sub-characteristics held up and which did not?
a: Fault tolerance held up: the system kept operating despite the disk fault. Recoverability fell short, because data was lost and re-establishing service took 2 hours, and availability suffered during that time. The fixes differ: recoverability needs protected, frequent recovery points and faster restore, not more disk mirroring.

q: An attacker logs in with a stolen password and changes another customer's delivery address. Which security sub-characteristics are broken?
a: Authenticity, because the identity was not the one claimed, and integrity, because data was changed without authorisation. Accountability also suffers, since the logs attribute the action to the victim. Stronger authentication addresses authenticity; checking that a user may modify **that** record addresses integrity.

q: A change to the tax calculation breaks three unrelated screens, and nobody can tell from the logs why. Which maintainability sub-characteristics are weak, and what would you fix first?
a: Modularity is weak, because a change in one component affected others, and so is analyzability, because the team cannot diagnose the fault or predict the impact of a change. Testability is probably weak too, since no test caught it. Isolate the tax logic behind an interface first to contain future changes, then improve logging to make faults diagnosable.

q: A start-up has 3 months to launch before a competitor and expects to rewrite the product within 18 months. A teammate insists on a fully modular, horizontally scalable design. Do you agree?
a: Mostly not. The business qualities here, a short time to market and a short projected lifetime, reduce the value of upfront investment in modifiability and scalability. Build the simplest design that meets the launch-critical qualities, keeping clean boundaries where they cost little. If the product is expected to live long or grow suddenly, the answer changes.

q: A government records system must run for 15 years across several hardware refreshes. Which product qualities gain priority, and what do you give up?
a: A long projected lifetime raises the priority of modifiability, scalability and portability, so the system survives changes in platform and demand. You give up some time to market and spend more upfront on abstraction and standard interfaces. With a short lifetime, the same investment would be hard to justify.

q: A product installs in one click, but users cannot complete their main task. Which quality models explain this?
a: Installability is a product quality under portability; completing the task is quality in use, especially effectiveness. Scoring well on one says nothing about the other. Evaluate both: product qualities describe the software, while quality in use judges it with real users in context.

q: A hospital group's enterprise architecture mandates one identity provider and an approved set of hosting regions. You are solution architect for a new telemedicine app, and a developer has already produced class diagrams and picked libraries. (a) Which decisions here belong to EA, SA and detailed design? (b) The developer's design skips the identity provider to save time. What do you do?
a: (a) The identity provider and hosting regions are EA decisions: strategic direction that constrains the solution. How the app's components collaborate to meet its qualities, and how it integrates with the identity provider, is solution architecture. Classes and libraries are detailed design, and they must fit inside the SA. (b) Align the design with EA. Bypassing the mandated identity provider breaks an enterprise constraint and creates a separate set of credentials to secure. Redesign the integration, or raise a justified exception with the enterprise architect if a requirement truly cannot be met. Record the decision either way.

q: A brilliant architect rarely attends team meetings. The team cannot build the design within budget and keeps asking him how two components should interact. Critique the situation and propose remedies.
a: This combines several failure patterns: an ivory-tower architect, an absent architect during construction, and a 'perfect' architecture that exceeds cost constraints, so the solution is not viable. A good architect earns the team's trust, documents an implementable architecture and its rationale, supports detailed design and construction, and leaves the team able to proceed without him. Remedies: re-evaluate the options against the budget and skills, document the component interactions and decisions, and hold regular design sessions with the team.

q: A mobile banking app must show balances within 1 s for 95% of requests. Security wants step-up authentication on every screen. (a) Name the quality relationship. (b) Write two utility-tree leaves with plausible ranks. (c) Propose a resolution and say what you give up.
a: (a) An inverse relationship between security (authenticity, confidentiality) and performance efficiency and usability, under this design. (b) For example: 'balance view returns within 1 s for 95% of requests at peak' (H,M), and 'a transfer above a set amount requires a second factor before it executes' (H,L). (c) Apply step-up authentication to risky operations such as transfers and payee changes, not to every screen, so balance views stay fast. You give up some protection on low-risk screens. The utility-tree ranking makes that trade-off explicit and reviewable.

q: A flash-sale platform expects 50,000 users in the first 10 minutes, takes payment through one external gateway, and changes its catalogue daily. Build a utility-tree fragment with three leaves, rank them, and say which drives the architecture first.
a: Leaves, for example: Performance: 'product page under 2 s for 95% of requests at 50,000 users in 10 minutes' (H,H). Availability: 'if the payment gateway times out, orders are held and confirmed within 5 minutes without double charging' (H,H). Modifiability: 'a catalogue change is published in under 1 hour without a deployment' (M,L). The high-importance, high-risk leaves come first: peak performance and payment failure handling shape the structure. The catalogue leaf can be met with known techniques. Evaluate the architecture by whether it makes each high-ranked scenario achievable.

q: A teammate says the only security requirement for a payments system is confidentiality, so TLS plus encrypted storage is enough. Do you agree? Use the ISO 25010 security sub-characteristics.
a: Disagree. TLS and encryption mainly address confidentiality and part of integrity. Payments also need integrity of stored amounts, authenticity (the payer is who they claim), non-repudiation (a customer cannot credibly deny a transfer they made) and accountability (each action is traced to one user). Each needs different mechanisms, such as strong authentication, signed or well-audited transactions, and per-user audit logs. Prioritise them with measurable scenarios rather than one blanket control.

q: Your firm has built five online-banking portals and is asked for a sixth, for a new bank. Separately, it is asked to architect a first-of-its-kind drone-delivery control system. How does your approach differ?
a: For the sixth portal, lean heavily on reuse: earlier solutions, reference patterns and a banking reference architecture, while checking that they fit this bank's requirements. For the drone system there is no close precedent, so rely more on method and on assets that only partly apply, and on intuition backed by more validation. The risk also differs: reuse risks carrying over assumptions that no longer fit, while an innovative design risks unproven decisions.

q: A team adopts a published retail e-commerce reference architecture for a B2B procurement system with multi-level approvals. What do they gain, and what must they check?
a: They gain a proven structure that bundles many patterns, which cuts logical design effort. A reference architecture is tied to its domain, though, so check its fit: B2B approval workflows and integration with buyers' systems may not appear in a retail reference at all. Keep what fits, add patterns for the gaps, and record where you departed from the reference.

q: Staff on the internal network need controlled internet access, and internet customers need to reach the company's web servers. Which kind of proxy fits each, and what does each hide?
a: Staff need a forward proxy: it gives firewall-restricted internal clients internet access and hides the clients' identity. Customers need a reverse proxy, typically in the DMZ, which fronts the internal servers and hides theirs. Using one for the other's job would expose the wrong side.

q: A design puts the web server, application server and database all in the DMZ 'to keep latency low'. Critique it.
a: Everything is now exposed in the outer zone, so compromising the web server gives direct reach to the application and the data. Keep only the internet-facing reverse proxy or web tier in the DMZ, put the application and database servers behind an inner firewall, and permit only the traffic each needs. The cost is an extra network boundary and more firewall rules to manage, which buys a much smaller blast radius.

q: A field-inspection app must keep working in areas with no mobile signal and sync later. Thick or thin client, and what design questions does that raise?
a: A thick client, because it needs local logic and storage to work offline. That raises the client-server design questions: how to split logic between client and server, how to manage state and reconcile changes made offline, and how to authenticate and authorise without a live connection. You give up easy updates and accept more data on devices, which must be protected.

q: A ride-hailing platform runs in two data centres. During a network partition between them, which operations would you let answer with possibly stale data, and which would you make wait or reject: showing nearby drivers, updating a profile photo, charging the rider's card?
a: Nearby drivers and profile photos can favour availability: slightly stale data is acceptable and reconciles later. Charging the card favours consistency: it should wait or fail rather than risk a double or lost charge. CAP is applied per operation during a partition, so state the acceptable staleness for each one rather than choosing by database label.

q: A teammate says: 'Our database is ACID, so it stays consistent even when the two regions lose contact.' Do you agree?
a: No. ACID consistency means a transaction preserves the database's rules; CAP consistency means all nodes behave like one up-to-date copy during a partition. An ACID label says nothing about what the system does when regions cannot communicate. Check the product's replication and partition behaviour, and decide per operation whether to reject requests or serve stale data.

q: A team picks a NoSQL document store for an invoicing system 'because NoSQL scales horizontally and SQL doesn't'. Invoices need atomic updates across customer, invoice and ledger records. Critique the choice.
a: The reasoning uses a label, not the requirement. The lecture presents horizontal NoSQL and vertical SQL scaling as tendencies, not guarantees. The deciding need here is coordinated multi-record updates, which a relational ACID store supports directly. Check the expected volume and each product's actual transaction and scaling options. If volume were huge and the data naturally document-shaped, the balance could change.

q: A company must push 2 GB software updates to 20,000 branch PCs over thin WAN links. Would a peer-to-peer style fit, and what concerns would you raise?
a: It can fit: peers act as both clients and servers, so branches share pieces locally instead of all downloading from the centre (the BitTorrent pattern). Raise the style's concerns: authenticating and authorising peers, keeping updates consistent and untampered across peers, and the discovery service peers still rely on. If the links could handle a central download, a simpler client-server distribution avoids those problems.

q: An order service must (a) hand each payment job to exactly one of several payment workers and (b) tell inventory, email and analytics that an order was placed. Which messaging style suits each?
a: (a) A point-to-point queue: each message goes to one consumer, so workers share the jobs. (b) Publish/subscribe: each subscriber gets the event, and new subscribers can be added without changing the order service. In both cases delivery depends on configuration: use persistent messages, acknowledgements and durable subscriptions if consumers can be offline.

q: Management wants a near-real-time sales dashboard combining three regional databases. An engineer proposes nightly FTP exports. Do you agree?
a: No. File-level data flow suits large scheduled batches and legacy systems with few options; real-time reporting and dashboards are a database-level use case (views, federation or replication). The trade-off is that database-level integration couples you to the source schemas and needs database access. If the regions can only export files, you are forced to file level and must accept stale data.

q: A 25-year-old application has no API, its source code is lost, and the business wants its data on a new web portal next quarter. What integration do you choose, and what are the risks?
a: Presentation-level integration (screen scraping) is the realistic choice: it suits extending a legacy system to the web without source code. It is fragile, though: any screen change breaks it, and it is slow and limited to what the screens show. If its database turns out to be accessible, database-level data flow would be more robust.

q: Checkout calls fraud check, inventory, loyalty points and email synchronously, one after another. The loyalty service is often slow, and checkout times out. What would you change?
a: Keep fraud check and inventory as call-and-return, because the checkout result depends on them. Move loyalty and email to event-based messaging so a slow service no longer holds checkout. Synchronous calls couple the caller to the callee in time, while events decouple them. The cost is extra complexity and loyalty points that update a little later, so add retries and failure handling for the asynchronous path.

q: A news site's application servers run at 90% CPU, mostly serving images and scripts, and readers abroad see slow page loads. What would you change, following the web reference architecture?
a: Move static content to object storage and serve it through a content delivery network. This takes static load off the application servers, which are left for dynamic content, and serves readers from the nearest edge location. It does not speed up slow dynamic pages, and updated content must reach the edge copies.

q: An e-commerce site keeps shopping carts in web-server memory. During a scale-in event, customers lose their carts. Diagnose and fix.
a: The cart state lives in the instance that was removed. As in the e-commerce reference, put carts in a persistent session store that survives instance loss. Keep volatile session data and catalogue caching in a fast in-memory store. The cost is another component to run and a network hop per cart access, and in return any instance can serve any customer.

q: A bank moves from server-rendered pages to a single-page app calling APIs. A developer proposes moving the transfer-limit check into the browser to save a round trip. Do you agree?
a: No. In a client-centric architecture, rendering and interaction move to the client, but server-side services must still enforce business rules and protect data, because client code can be bypassed. A browser-side check is fine for quick feedback, as long as the server repeats it.

q: A retail system's search service is overloaded at peak, its order table has grown to 2 billion rows, and the promotions and payments teams keep blocking each other's releases. Which scale-cube axis addresses each problem?
a: Search load: the X axis, cloning more identical instances behind a load balancer. The huge order table: the Z axis, partitioning data (for example by customer) so each instance handles a subset. The team collisions: the Y axis, splitting by function into separate services. Each has a cost: X needs stateless instances, Z complicates queries across partitions, and Y adds distributed operations.

q: A team lists service instance addresses in configuration files. After auto-scaling is switched on, calls fail intermittently. Diagnose and fix.
a: Instances are now ephemeral: new ones are missing from the files and removed ones are still being called. Add service discovery: clients call a router at a well-known location, which looks up available instances in a service registry. The registry then becomes critical infrastructure and needs its own high availability.

q: All 40 integrations in a bank flow through one ESB instance, and an ESB upgrade took every channel offline for an evening. What risk did this expose, and what would you consider?
a: The broker style's main risk: the central broker is a single point of failure and a potential bottleneck. Make the broker redundant and upgradable without an outage, and consider moving integrations that need no central orchestration to direct or event-based links. You give up some central governance in exchange for resilience.

q: A 10-person team with one product and weekly releases is told to split its layered monolith into 30 microservices. Do you agree?
a: Probably not yet. Microservices give independently deployable, scalable vertical slices, but they bring a dense web of dependencies and need service discovery, gateways and automation. With one team and a manageable release pace, that operational cost likely outweighs the benefit. Modularise the monolith first, and split out a service when a part needs independent scaling or more teams join.

q: You must run 200 small instances of the same Linux service, and also host a legacy application that needs its own OS kernel version. Containers or VMs for each?
a: Containers for the 200 instances: they share the host kernel and package only the application and its dependencies, so they are lighter and denser. A VM for the legacy application, because it needs its own guest OS. The trade-off is isolation: a VM has a guest OS boundary, while containers share one kernel.

q: A SaaS payroll provider hosts 300 client companies on shared infrastructure, and load spikes at each month end. Which cloud property addresses which concern?
a: Multitenancy addresses sharing: each company's workloads and data must stay isolated in the common environment. Elasticity addresses the spike: resources are provisioned up for month end and back down afterwards. They interact: elastic capacity without good tenant isolation lets one tenant's spike degrade the others.

q: An image-thumbnail job runs a few hundred times a day, with occasional bursts of several thousand. Serverless functions or always-on containers?
a: Serverless fits: you supply the function and the platform runs and scales it, so you manage no servers and are not paying for idle capacity between bursts. You give up control over the runtime environment. If the load became steady and high, re-examine whether always-on instances are better value.

q: A service blocks one thread per request while calling a slow partner API. Under peak load it stops responding entirely. What would the Reactive Manifesto suggest?
a: Use asynchronous message passing, so a slow partner does not tie up a thread per request. This gives loose coupling and isolation, keeping the service responsive under varying load (elastic) and when the partner fails (resilient). The cost is a more complex programming and failure-handling model.

q: An architect presents one large diagram mixing classes, servers, network zones and business process steps. Operations staff and developers both say it doesn't answer their questions. What would you change?
a: Split it into views aimed at each stakeholder's concerns, as ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 suggests: a physical or deployment view for operations, a development view for programmers, a logical view for functionality and a process view for performance. Tie them together with key scenarios. The cost is keeping several views consistent, which the scenarios help with.

q: Three concerns are raised: an integrator asks about throughput between concurrent processes; a system engineer asks how components are installed across sites; programmers ask how code modules are organised for testing. Which 4+1 view answers each?
a: The process view answers the integrator (performance, throughput, concurrency). The physical view answers the system engineer (topology, installation, delivery). The development view answers the programmers (code organisation, testing). Scenarios then check that the three views describe the same system.

q: A team defines a deployment viewpoint but supplies no deployment view. What is missing?
a: The viewpoint sets the conventions and concerns; the view applies them to this system. The team still needs the actual mapping of components and artifacts to nodes, with the relevant connections.

q: A security auditor asks which components run in the DMZ and which can talk to the database. Which viewpoint and notation would you use?
a: The deployment viewpoint, using UML deployment diagrams, to map logical components to physical nodes. Add the infrastructure viewpoint, a network diagram, to show zones and permitted connections. A logical component diagram alone cannot answer the question, because it doesn't say where anything runs.

q: A retailer's legacy inventory system offers only a nightly CSV export and read access to its database. A new web shop needs stock levels no more than 1 minute old, synchronous order placement, and order notifications to email, SMS and analytics. (a) Choose a communication style and integration level for each need. (b) The inventory team then forbids direct database access. What changes?
a: (a) Stock: database-level data flow (replication or a view), because 1-minute freshness rules out the nightly file. Orders: application-level call and return through a web service, because the customer needs an immediate result. Notifications: publish/subscribe, so email, SMS and analytics subscribe independently and new channels need no change to the order service. Structurally, use a tiered client-server design with a reverse proxy in the DMZ. (b) Without database access, only the file export remains. Either negotiate an application-level interface on the inventory system or accept stale stock data and show availability as approximate. Document this as a constraint-driven decision with its business impact.

q: A concert-ticketing platform runs in two regions. During an on-sale for 20,000 seats, the regions lose contact for 2 minutes. Which operations favour availability and which favour consistency? What does the customer see, and does an ACID database settle the question?
a: Browsing events and seat maps can favour availability and accept briefly stale seat maps. Seat reservation and payment must favour consistency, or two regions could sell the same seat. During the partition, those operations wait or are refused in the region that cannot coordinate, and the customer sees a 'try again' or queue message. Reconcile holds when the link returns. ACID transactions guarantee rules within a transaction, but say nothing about partition behaviour, so the replication design must be checked separately.

q: A five-year-old monolith: during sales the catalogue gets 50 times the traffic of checkout; three teams work on it; a nightly report reads every table. Propose a decomposition using the scale cube and name two side effects to monitor.
a: Y axis: split by business capability (catalogue, checkout, accounts), each service owning its data, so teams deploy independently. X axis: clone the catalogue service heavily for sales peaks without scaling checkout. Z axis: partition order data later if it grows too large. Add an API gateway and service discovery. The nightly report can no longer read every table; feed it from events or replicas. Side effects to monitor: cross-service consistency (orders referring to changed catalogue data), and latency and failures across the new network call chains, which need tracing and timeouts.

q: Compare two organisations. A bank has 15 legacy core systems, and loan approval is a long process orchestrated across six of them. A start-up has one product, two teams and frequent releases. Would you lean towards broker/SOA or microservices for each, and why?
a: The bank leans towards SOA with a broker: layered services over the existing operational systems, with process orchestration in the integration layer, reusing enterprise services. Make the broker redundant, because it is a single point of failure and a bottleneck risk. The start-up leans towards a modular monolith now and microservices later: independent vertical slices with their own data favour agility, but only once the team can support discovery, gateways and automation. The deciding factors are the number of systems to integrate, the complexity of orchestration and the team's operational maturity.

q: A new payments platform is reviewed by an auditor (where card data flows and who can reach it), operations (servers, sites, failover) and developers (module structure, build). How would you document the architecture, and how do you keep the views consistent?
a: Follow 42010: list the stakeholders and their concerns, then choose viewpoints. Auditor: an information-structure view (class or ER model) for card data, plus deployment and infrastructure views showing zones and permitted connections. Operations: the physical or deployment view, with nodes, sites and failover paths. Developers: the development view and an application-structure view (packages, components). Use a process view for throughput and concurrency. Tie the views together with key scenarios such as 'authorise a card payment', and trace each scenario through every view.

q: An exam-results portal is idle most of the year, then 200,000 students log in during the first hour of results day. The results are personal data under strict regulation. Which reference-architecture options would you weigh, and what do you give up with each?
a: The demand profile calls for elasticity: capacity that scales up for one hour and back down. That favours public cloud with containers on an elastic platform, or serverless functions for the read-heavy results lookup, which scale without managed servers. Data sensitivity pushes the other way, towards private or hybrid deployment, keeping the results store in a controlled environment and putting only the elastic front end in public cloud. Serverless gives up runtime control, and private hosting gives up elasticity, forcing you to provision for the peak. Judge the options by availability on results day, security, cost and responsiveness under the spike, the Reactive goal.

q: A team's process document lists tasks such as 'design the database' and 'write tests', but not who does them, what each produces or when they happen. What is missing, and why does it matter?
a: It has the 'how' (activities and tasks) but not the 'who' (roles), the 'what' (work products) or the 'when' (phases and iterations). Without roles nobody owns the outputs, and without work products nobody can tell when a task is done or what the next task takes as input. Adding them turns a to-do list into a method that can be planned and reviewed.

q: A project manager plans to start architecture work in Construction, 'once there is some code to look at'. Critique the plan.
a: In the Unified Process, architecture effort peaks in Elaboration, because the key structural decisions and risks must be settled before heavy construction. Starting late means building on unvalidated assumptions and paying for rework. Architecture does continue into Construction, as detailing and refinement, but it should not start there.

q: While detailing the physical architecture, the team learns that the payment provider accepts only batch files. Does the method require starting again from requirements?
a: No full restart: architecting is iterative. Record the new constraint in the requirements and revisit the affected logical elements (the payment boundary and its control flow). Then update the physical design and record the decision. Only the parts the constraint touches need to change.

q: Stakeholder workshops for a hospital booking system included doctors, patients and the operations director only. What is missing, and what is likely to go wrong?
a: The technical stakeholders are missing: system administrators and the owners of external systems such as the patient-record and payment systems. Business stakeholders rarely state availability, operability and integration constraints, so those will surface late and force rework. The architect should make sure qualities and constraints are collected, not just features.

q: In a resort system, reservation agents work both at the central office and at each hotel's front desk, with different network access. How do you show them in the system context, and why?
a: Introduce a separate actor for each location, such as Central Office Reservation Agent and Hotel Reservation Agent. Each can then be placed, given its own data flows and reasoned about for connectivity and deployment. The cost is a slightly larger context diagram, in exchange for not hiding location-specific requirements.

q: Sales uses 'booking' to mean a confirmed, paid reservation, while operations uses it for any held slot. Why does the architect care?
a: Inconsistent terms lead to inconsistent requirements and data models: capacity counts, reports and integration messages would disagree about what a booking is. Capture a common vocabulary early and define each term once, because fixing it after the data model is built is far more expensive.

q: An NFR reads: 'Search shall respond in under 3 seconds.' What would you add before using it for sizing or testing?
a: The conditions: the workload (concurrent users, request mix, think time), the measurement boundary (server only or end to end), whether 3 s is an average or a percentile such as 90% of requests, the test environment, and the measurement period. Without them, two teams can test the same system and both claim compliance with different results.

q: Is 'supports 1000 concurrent users' enough to size the servers?
a: No. Specify what users do, their request mix and think time, and the required response times. A concurrent-user count alone does not determine the request rate or the work each request needs.

q: The functional outline for a reservation system lists only customer use cases. Later, operations asks how to cancel a stuck reservation. What went wrong?
a: Functional requirements should be outlined per actor in the system context, including technical users such as administrators and operators. Missing 'Administer Reservations' means the function and its data access are added late, causing rework. The outline should also confirm explicitly what is out of scope.

q: Search must be 99.9% available, and every other function 99%. What does this split let the architect do?
a: Give search extra redundancy and isolate it from the less critical functions, instead of paying for 99.9% across the whole system. The cost is a more complex deployment with separately scaled parts, which is worth it only if search can actually run independently of the 99% components.

q: For a ticketing system, which of these are architecturally significant, and why: (a) the colour of the 'print receipt' button; (b) handling 30,000 buyers in the first 5 minutes of a sale; (c) integration with a national ID service's fixed API; (d) a streaming library nobody on the team has used?
a: (b) is a critical quality (performance and scalability), (c) is a critical constraint, and (d) carries technical risk, so all three are significant and shape the structure. (a) is a detail with no architectural impact. Significant requirements are worth detailing first because they are costly to change later.

q: Rewrite 'the system shall be available' as a six-part availability scenario for a payment-gateway outage.
a: Source: the external payment gateway. Stimulus: it stops responding. Artifact: the checkout service. Environment: normal operation at peak load. Response: detect the failure, hold orders and tell customers that payment is pending. Response measure: detection within 30 s, no confirmed order lost, and checkout degraded for no more than 10 minutes. Each part now gives the architect something to design and test against.

q: Late in the project, a stakeholder asks to drop the 'check hotel availability' requirement. How does the Solution Architecture Document help?
a: Its traceability section links the requirement to the components, interfaces and decisions that satisfy it, so you can see what would be removed or simplified and estimate the impact. Handle the change through a change request and the review process, and record the outcome. Without traceability, the impact is guesswork.

q: IROne built a custom rules engine on the assumption of about 30 to 40 rules. A year later, marketing wants 400 rules editable by business users. What does the decision record tell you to do?
a: The recorded assumption no longer holds, so the decision must be reviewed. The recorded alternatives, such as buying a commercial rules engine that was overkill at 30 rules, may now be justified. Reassess against the new needs rather than switching automatically; this is why decisions record assumptions and alternatives as well as the choice.

q: A client buys a packaged reservation product that covers 70% of the required functions. How does this change where architecture effort goes?
a: Less effort goes into logical structure, because the package supplies much of it. More goes into the physical architecture: fitting and configuring the package, and integrating the remaining 30%. The risk shifts too: the package's constraints now limit the design, so record them as decisions.

q: A decision log entry reads only 'Decision: use a message queue for hotel integration.' What is wrong with it?
a: It lacks the issue, assumptions, alternatives and justification. Later teams cannot tell why the queue was chosen, what was rejected, or what change (in volume or latency needs, for instance) should trigger a review. Record the full Issue, Decision, Assumptions, Alternatives, Justification template.

q: For a 'Cancel Booking' use case: the customer's web page, the logic that coordinates the cancellation and refund rules, the link to the payment gateway, and the Booking record. Classify each and say how many controllers you would start with.
a: The web page is a boundary (to the primary actor). The payment gateway link is a boundary (to an external system). The coordinating logic is a control component, and the Booking record is an entity. Start with one controller for the use case, and split it into sub-controllers only if it becomes too complex.

q: A design has one 'ReservationManager' component that renders screens, applies rules, calls the hotel system and stores the data. What is wrong, in robustness-analysis terms?
a: It mixes boundary, control and entity responsibilities, so a change to a screen, a rule or the hotel interface affects one large component. Split it into a reservation UI and hotel-system interface (boundaries), a reserve-slot control, and the reservation entity. The cost is more components and interfaces, and in return changes stay local.

q: The architecture overview leaves out the payment system that appears in the system context. How should this be caught?
a: Trace every actor, external system and data flow from the system context into the overview: the payment system needs a boundary or integration-layer element. Starting the overview from the context makes such omissions visible, but only if someone checks it item by item.

q: The team doubts whether the rules engine can evaluate 40 rules within the 3-second search target. Is a verification meeting enough?
a: No. Verification reviews the outlined architecture for consistency and cross-cutting concerns; it cannot measure performance. This is a risk that calls for validation: build an architectural proof of concept, measure it against the 3 s target with a realistic load, and document the findings and recommendations.

q: A logical deployment model labels the application node '2 x 16-core, 64 GB'. A reviewer objects. Why?
a: Hardware and sizing are physical decisions. At the logical stage, nodes only say which kinds of node exist, in which locations, and what runs on them. Fixing hardware before the technology is chosen and the NFRs are sized commits the design early and without evidence.

q: Two teams will build components that call each other, and so far they have agreed only on component names. What must the detailed functional model add before they code?
a: Interfaces with operations and signatures, contracts (preconditions and postconditions) and the logical data model they exchange. Without these, each team will assume different behaviour and the mismatch appears at integration.

q: Logical 'Reservation Control' must meet 99.9% availability. Logical 'Reporting', 'Billing' and 'CRM' are all covered by one packaged product. Which logical-to-physical mapping applies to each, and what does each cost?
a: Reservation Control maps one to many: several physical instances, so one failure does not stop the service. That needs load balancing and state handling. The packaged product is many to one: one physical element realises several logical ones, which ties them to that product's release cycle and limits.

q: A team maps every logical component, including the hotel-system interfaces, to synchronous REST controllers. The hotel systems are reachable only through message queues. Critique the mapping.
a: Each logical element must be mapped to technology that meets its specification and constraints. A system-facing boundary to queue-only hotel systems should map to messaging (IROne used JMS), while person-facing boundaries map to the web tier. Record the mapping choice per element as a decision, rather than applying one technology everywhere.

q: IROne chose an application server product because the team already had skills in it. A new CTO says to always choose the cheapest licence. How do you respond?
a: Existing skills reduce delivery and operating risk, which is part of the solution's viability, so the cheapest licence may not be the cheapest solution once training, mistakes and slower delivery are counted. The decision record holds this justification. If the team's skills change or licence cost becomes dominant, revisit the decision.

q: Requirements: 1000 concurrent users and 99.9% search availability. A physical design has one web server and one application server, each sized for 1,200 users. Does it meet the NFRs?
a: Capacity may be enough, but availability is not met: each tier is a single point of failure. Use at least two nodes per tier, sized so that the survivors still handle 1000 users when one fails. Then confirm availability and capacity with the real workload.

q: The requirements specify web-service integration, but the physical example uses JMS. What should the architect do?
a: Treat it as a traceability issue. Confirm whether an approved decision changed the requirement or an adapter satisfies it; otherwise revise the physical design. The example's technology mapping alone is not evidence of compliance.

q: The integration endpoint table shows client to web over HTTPS/HTML, and application to hotel systems over messaging with XML, marked 'transformation: yes'. What work does that flag create?
a: An adapter that maps the application's structures to the hotel systems' formats and meanings, which must be specified and tested. The flag says mapping is needed; it does not define it. Use of XML or messaging alone does not prove a transformation is needed.

q: The same logical design must be redeployed as containerised microservices. What changes and what stays?
a: The logical functional model (components, interfaces, contracts) largely stays. The physical deployment changes: nodes become containers grouped into services, such as a reservation service with its own database and a separate integration service. Endpoints, sizing and the deployment mapping must be redone and validated against the NFRs.

q: A clinic chain wants online booking within 6 months: 40 clinics, about 2,000 concurrent users at 8 am, and integration with a patient-record system that only accepts batch files overnight. (a) Pick three architecturally significant requirements and justify each. (b) Write one as a six-part scenario. (c) What decision would you record about the patient-record integration?
a: (a) The 8 am peak of 2,000 concurrent users is a critical quality, because it drives capacity and scaling. The overnight-only patient-record interface is a critical constraint. Booking itself is critical functionality, without which there is no viable system. (b) Source: 2,000 patients; stimulus: book an appointment; artifact: booking service; environment: the 8 am peak; response: the slot is confirmed; measure: 90% of confirmations within 3 s. (c) Issue: bookings must reach patient records, but only overnight batch is possible. Decision: store bookings in the booking system and export them nightly. Assumptions: clinics can tolerate next-day sync. Alternatives: real-time integration, which is not offered. Justification: it meets the constraint. Revisit if same-day record access becomes a requirement.

q: A requirements document says: 'The system must be fast, secure and user-friendly and support 1000 users.' It lists only customer use cases. As architect, critique it and say what you would do in Define Requirements.
a: None of the qualities are measurable, the user count gives no request mix or think time, and technical users and external systems are missing. Collect requests from technical stakeholders too (administrators, owners of external systems). Build a glossary and a system context with actors per location. Outline functional requirements per actor, including administration, and NFRs with targets and conditions. Prioritise the architecturally significant ones and detail them as use cases and six-part scenarios. Record them in the SAD with traceability, and review with stakeholders.

q: For a 'Transfer Ticket' use case (an owner transfers a ticket to a friend, the system checks transfer rules and notifies an external venue system), derive the boundary, control and entity components, then propose a physical mapping that supports high availability.
a: Boundaries: the transfer UI (owner) and the venue-system interface (external). Control: Transfer Ticket control, which coordinates the rules check, possibly using a rules component. Entities: Ticket and Transfer record. Physical mapping: the UI to the web tier; the control to a stateless application component deployed one to many across several instances; the venue interface to messaging, so venue outages don't block transfers; the entities to a persistent store with redundancy. Record each choice as a decision and check it against the availability target.

q: Logical model: web, application, rules and integration nodes at the central office. NFRs: 1000 concurrent users with 99.9% availability. A benchmark shows one application node handles 400 users at the response target. Size the physical application tier and explain your mapping.
a: Capacity alone needs 1000 / 400 = 2.5, so 3 nodes. To survive one node failure, the survivors must still carry 1000 users, so 4 nodes (3 survivors x 400 = 1,200). That is a one-to-many mapping of the logical application node, which requires stateless components or shared session state, and a load balancer. Confirm the 400-user figure with the production request mix, since benchmarks do not scale perfectly. Then specify the hardware, deployment units and endpoints.

q: A validation proof of concept shows the integration server handles 50 messages/s, but the peak need is 120 messages/s. How does this finding flow through the method, and what options would you weigh?
a: Validation documents the finding, its risk and recommendations, traced to the NFR it threatens. Options: deploy the integration node one to many (three instances give about 150 messages/s if it scales, which must be measured), batch or queue messages to smooth the peak if a short delay is acceptable, or reduce the work per message. Record the chosen option as a decision with its assumptions, update the SAD and review it with stakeholders. Repeat validation until the risk is acceptable.

q: In a hospital lab system: (a) a nurse views results for a patient not in her care; (b) a script changes a stored potassium value; (c) ransomware locks the system for 6 hours. Classify each against CIA and say which you would protect hardest.
a: (a) Confidentiality, (b) integrity, (c) availability. Integrity is arguably the most dangerous here, because a silently wrong value leads to wrong treatment, while availability matters for emergencies. Rank them per asset through risk assessment, rather than assuming confidentiality always comes first.

q: A team says: 'We passed a penetration test at launch, so the system is secure.' Do you agree?
a: No. Security means **preserving** confidentiality, integrity and availability over time, while threats, vulnerabilities and the system itself keep changing. A test at launch is one snapshot. Keep assessing and treating risk as an ongoing loop, and repeat testing after significant changes.

q: Security is added after the architecture is built, by placing a firewall in front of the system. What problems does this cause?
a: The firewall protects only the network path it sits on. Data at rest, insider access and every other path to the data stay unprotected, and logging in alone does not secure all of them. Controls such as zoning, encryption and access control shape the architecture, so retrofitting them costs more than capturing security requirements and reviewing the design from the start.

q: A team buys a web application firewall before identifying any assets or threats, then asks 'Are we safe now?' What did they skip, and what is the consequence?
a: They skipped scoping and risk assessment (identification, analysis, evaluation) and went straight to treatment. They cannot tell whether the control addresses their highest risks, or what residual risk remains. Go back, assess, and then judge whether the firewall was the right treatment, as part of an ongoing process.

q: A threat report says ransomware gangs are targeting the logistics sector. Your warehouse system is isolated, fully patched and has offline backups. Is your risk high?
a: Not necessarily. Risk needs a threat, an exploitable vulnerability, an asset and a harmful consequence. Patching and isolation reduce the vulnerability, and offline backups reduce the consequence, so the threat alone does not make the risk high. Some residual risk remains (unknown flaws, insiders), and the assessment must be repeated as conditions change.

q: To protect a plant's control network, an engineer installs a data diode so data can only flow out to the corporate network. Has the risk been eliminated?
a: No, it has been reduced. The diode removes the inbound network path, but other paths still need evaluating: maintenance laptops, removable media and vendor access. Controls reduce risk; they need not remove it, so record the residual risk.

q: Attackers compromise a clinic receptionist's PC, which holds no patient data. Why should the incident team treat this seriously?
a: The PC is a stepping stone: attackers use footholds like this to pivot across network segments to the crown jewels, here the patient records (the SingHealth pattern). Contain it as if the records were at risk, and reduce the number of reachable paths from workstations through segmentation and least privilege.

q: A mobile banking API returns full account details for any account number once the caller is logged in. Write the risk scenario and name the STRIDE category.
a: An authenticated attacker (threat) exploits the missing per-account authorisation check (vulnerability) to read other customers' account data (asset), causing disclosure of confidential financial data (consequence). STRIDE: information disclosure, which breaks confidentiality; reaching data beyond one's rights is also elevation of privilege. The fix is to authorise every request against the specific account.

q: Customers claim they never placed certain large orders, and the logs cannot show otherwise. Which STRIDE threat is this, which objective is broken, and what would you add?
a: Repudiation, which breaks non-repudiation. Add evidence that ties each action to an authenticated identity, such as digitally signed transactions or protected audit logs. Non-repudiation provides proof to challenge a denial; it does not make denial impossible.

q: A company holds 400 data sets and has a small security budget. How should it focus its protection?
a: Identify the small set of most critical data (the crown jewels) and give each one a custodian responsible for it. Protect those, and the stepping stones that lead to them, first. Spreading the budget evenly across all 400 would leave the data that matters most under-protected.

q: Flaw A has a public exploit, needs only a browser and no login, and exposes one user's profile. Flaw B needs an insider administrator and custom tools, but can destroy the whole database. Score them roughly with DREAD and say which you would fix first.
a: A: discoverability, reproducibility and exploitability near 10, affected users and damage low to medium, so high likelihood and moderate impact. B: discoverability, reproducibility and exploitability low, affected users and damage 10, so low likelihood and catastrophic impact. DREAD totals may put A first, and it is cheap to fix. B's catastrophic impact still needs an explicit decision against the organisation's tolerance, because DREAD scores rank concerns but are not probabilities.

q: A manager wants every risk reported to the board as a single DREAD number. A colleague prefers a 3-by-3 likelihood and impact matrix. Which would you use, and why?
a: Use both, for different audiences. DREAD's factor scores help the technical team rank and compare flaws. The matrix gives a quick low, medium or high rating that is easier to communicate. Neither is a measured probability, so state the scoring criteria behind them.

q: A rare event could destroy all patient records. Does a Low matrix cell settle the treatment decision?
a: No. The matrix uses chosen scoring criteria. Review the severe consequence and organisational tolerance, then decide treatment and record residual risk rather than treating the colour as automatic acceptance.

q: A retailer buys cyber insurance, outsources card processing, and then declares card-data risk 'handled'. Do you agree?
a: Only partly. Insurance transfers part of the financial impact, and outsourcing reduces the card data the retailer holds. Neither removes operational disruption, reputational harm or the retailer's accountability, and some residual risk stays in-house. Record that residual risk and decide whether it is within tolerance.

q: An internal wiki with little traffic has an unpatched minor flaw. The fix needs a $50,000 platform upgrade. When could you accept the risk, and what must you record?
a: Accept it if assessment shows the risk falls within the organisation's tolerance, for example low impact and no access from outside. Record the decision, its owner and the conditions that would trigger a review, such as the wiki starting to hold sensitive data. A cheap compensating control, such as restricting access, may reduce the risk further.

q: A bank's 'save card for later' feature on a niche product creates serious exposure and earns little revenue. Mitigate or avoid?
a: Avoid: dropping the feature removes the activity that creates the risk, at little business cost. Mitigation with encryption and access control would add ongoing cost and still leave residual risk. If the feature mattered commercially, mitigation would be the better choice.

q: A consultant hands a start-up the full catalogue of about 1,000 security controls and says to implement them all. How do you respond?
a: No. Controls have costs and limits on where they apply. Start with mandatory obligations and any required baseline, then use risk assessment to select and justify additional controls. A catalogue offers choices, not a checklist to complete.

q: A 20-person firm with no security staff asks where to start. Risk assessment or a hygiene list?
a: Start with cyber hygiene, such as the CSA Essentials (asset inventory, authorised software, patching, restricted admin rights, breach detection, access control including MFA). It builds a foundation without a full assessment of each risk. Add risk assessment for the systems holding its crown jewels. Hygiene complements risk assessment; it does not prove the firm is safe.

q: The baseline mandates MFA for all administrator access on a comply-or-explain basis. A legacy controller cannot support MFA. What do you do?
a: Explain: document why the control cannot be applied and what alternative reduces the risk, such as reaching the controller only through an MFA-protected jump host on a segregated admin network. Get the exception approved and set a review date. Simply ignoring the control is not an option under comply-or-explain.

q: For a card-payment kiosk, classify each control by type and category: tamper-evident seals, a quarterly log review, an IDS, and restoring from backup.
a: Tamper-evident seals: physical, detective (and deterrent). Quarterly log review: administrative, detective. IDS: technical, detective. Restore from backup: technical, corrective. Three of the four are detective, so check that preventive controls also exist.

q: A design's control list is firewall, encryption, MFA and a security policy. What is wrong with this mix?
a: Every control is preventive. If prevention fails, nothing detects the breach or recovers from it. Add detective controls (IDS, log review) and corrective ones (tested backups, incident response). Checking both the type and the category of each control exposes this kind of gap.

q: A legacy system cannot be patched, so the team isolates it on its own segment. Which category?
a: Compensating: it substitutes for the missing primary control (patching) to still reduce the risk.

q: A team encrypts a 2 GB nightly backup directly with the recipient's RSA public key. Critique it and propose a better scheme.
a: Public-key operations are relatively costly and suit key establishment, not bulk data. Encrypt the backup with a random symmetric key, then protect that key with the recipient's public key, so only the private-key holder can recover it. Protect the private key well, because it now unlocks every backup.

q: Choose a mechanism for each: (a) internal services that share a secret must detect tampered messages; (b) a bank must later prove that a customer authorised a transfer; (c) users download an installer and compare it with a digest published on the same website, which may be compromised.
a: (a) HMAC: shared-secret integrity and authentication of a key holder. (b) A digital signature with the customer's private key, because HMAC cannot provide non-repudiation when both sides hold the secret. (c) A digest from the same compromised site is worthless, since the attacker can replace both files. Use a signature verified with a trusted public key, or a digest from a trusted channel.

q: A client accepts any certificate whose subject matches the server's name, without checking who issued it. What attack does this allow?
a: An attacker can present their own certificate with the same subject name and impersonate the server (spoofing, then reading or altering traffic). A certificate binds a key to a subject only through the issuer's signature. Verify that signature up to a trusted CA before trusting the identity.

q: An attacker can rewrite a file and its stored SHA-256 digest. Has the digest protected integrity?
a: No. The attacker can recompute an unkeyed digest. Use a trusted comparison value, an HMAC with a protected shared key, or a verified digital signature, according to the trust model.

q: An attacker has recorded two years of a server's TLS traffic and now steals the server's long-term private key. Under which key exchange can the past traffic be decrypted?
a: With RSA key transport, yes: the session keys were sent encrypted with that key, so all the recorded traffic opens. With authenticated ephemeral Diffie-Hellman whose session secrets were erased, no: that is forward secrecy. Prefer ephemeral key agreement, and protect long-term keys in an HSM.

q: TLS terminates at a load balancer in the DMZ, and traffic to the application server is re-encrypted with a second TLS hop. A teammate says passwords are protected end to end. Do you agree?
a: No. Each TLS connection protects only between its own endpoints, so the password is plaintext inside the load balancer in the DMZ. If that exposure is unacceptable, encrypt the password field for the final consumer (with a nonce against replay), or terminate TLS at the application server. Otherwise, treat the load balancer as part of the trust boundary and harden it.

q: A vendor needs remote access to maintain one internal server. Where would you terminate their SSL VPN, and what else must you control?
a: Terminating in the DMZ keeps the exposed endpoint outside the inner boundary, and the inner firewall then allows only that one server. Terminating internally keeps keys deeper inside but bypasses DMZ inspection. Either way, the VPN gives only a tunnel: you still need strong vendor authentication, authorisation limited to that server, and logging of the session.

q: A developer generates session keys with the language's standard random function, seeded with the current time. What is the problem?
a: The sequence is deterministic: the same seed repeats the same output, and an attacker who can guess the time can reproduce the keys. Use a cryptographic random generator with enough entropy, or authenticated key agreement, for session keys.

q: A bank offers three login options: (a) password plus a one-time code from a hardware token; (b) fingerprint plus a key bound to the phone; (c) password plus a security question. Which are true multi-factor?
a: (a) is multi-factor: something you know plus something you have. (b) is multi-factor: something you are plus something you have. (c) is a single factor, because both are knowledge. MFA needs independent factor types, not just more secrets.

q: Ransomware on one office PC reached the database servers within an hour. What design flaw does this suggest, and what is the fix?
a: A flat network: once inside, any host could reach the others. Segregate it into zones (user, DMZ, internal, development) with controlled connections, so a compromised PC has few reachable targets, and move administration to an out-of-band network. Permitted paths still need authentication and authorisation.

q: A vendor installs an outbound remote-desktop tool on a server so they can support it. The firewall blocks all inbound traffic. Is the server safe from outside access?
a: No. The tool opens a connection from the inside, which the inbound rules don't stop, and the vendor's service becomes a path into the network. Route vendor access through a controlled, authenticated and logged path, such as a VPN or jump host on the admin network, and block unapproved outbound remote tools.

q: Does requiring both a password and a PIN give two-factor authentication?
a: No. Both are knowledge factors. Combine independent types, such as a password with possession of an OTP token, to obtain multiple factors.

q: A patient-records API sits behind an inline IPS that could block attacks, but false positives would also block clinicians. Would you run it in blocking mode or as an alerting IDS?
a: It depends on the cost of a false block. Here, blocking legitimate clinicians hurts availability for patient care, so start in alerting (IDS) mode, tune the rules, and enable blocking only for well-understood signatures. On a public edge where a false block costs little, inline blocking is easier to justify.

q: Traffic to an application server is end-to-end encrypted, and you suspect an attacker is modifying files on it. HIDS or NIDS?
a: A HIDS: it runs on the host and watches system calls, file-system changes and host activity, which encrypted network traffic hides from a network sensor. The cost is an agent to deploy and maintain on each protected host.

q: Ransomware encrypted both production and the online backups mounted on the same network. What should the backup design have included?
a: Offline copies, access controls on the backup system, WORM retention where appropriate, regularly tested restores, and golden images to rebuild systems. WORM stops rewriting but not theft, and it doesn't prove the copy was clean, so test restores as well.

q: An IDS alerts that a staff account is uploading large volumes of data to an unknown external host at 3 am. Which reacting controls apply, and what is the risk of using them?
a: Revoke or suspend the account's access, block the destination with an IPS or firewall rule, and stop the exfiltration. The risk is a false positive, such as a legitimate overnight transfer, disrupting work. Confirm quickly and keep the response proportionate.

q: A web app checks the user's role at login and stores 'isAdmin = true' in the session for 8 hours. An administrator is dismissed at 10 am. Which principle is broken, and what is the risk?
a: Complete mediation. The cached decision keeps the revoked rights working for up to 8 hours. Check every access against current permissions. The cost is a permission lookup per request, which is the price of revocation taking effect immediately.

q: A service account has superuser rights 'for convenience'. Which principle and what harm?
a: Least privilege: if the account is exploited the attacker inherits superuser power; grant only network, one table read and log write.

q: A public API faces DDoS risk, and its only protection is a perimeter firewall. Propose a defence-in-depth arrangement.
a: Layer the controls: DNS and a content delivery edge to absorb volume, a web application firewall, an API gateway that throttles requests, load balancing with auto-scaling, and application servers in private subnets. Protect the data behind them with access control and encryption. Each layer catches some of what passes the one before. The cost is more components to configure and pay for.

q: Production and test share one encryption key and one admin jump host 'to keep things simple'. Which principle is broken, and what is the risk?
a: Least common mechanism: shared mechanisms become channels between environments. Compromising the weaker test environment exposes the production key and the production admin path. Use separate keys per purpose and environment, and a dedicated admin path for production.

q: A pharmacy chain's online prescription portal serves 200,000 patients. The web tier in the DMZ reads a records database, a vendor has remote support access, and the budget covers three new controls this year. (a) Identify a crown jewel and a stepping stone. (b) Write two risk scenarios and rate them. (c) Choose a treatment for each and three controls, justifying the mix of types and categories. (d) State the residual risk.
a: (a) Crown jewel: patient prescription records. Stepping stones: the DMZ web server and the vendor's remote access path. (b) 'An attacker exploits the vendor's remote access to reach the records database and disclose prescriptions': medium likelihood, high impact. 'An attacker exploits a web-tier flaw and pivots to the database': medium likelihood, high impact. (c) Mitigate both. Controls: MFA-protected, logged vendor access through a jump host (technical, preventive and detective); segmentation with an inner firewall that allows only required web-to-database traffic (technical, preventive); centralised log review with alerting (administrative and technical, detective). (d) Residual: unknown application flaws and insider misuse. Record them, accept them within tolerance, and revisit next year.

q: Threat-model a mobile banking transfer: phone app, then API gateway, then transfer service, then core banking system. For each of three trust boundaries, give the most likely STRIDE threat, the objective it breaks and a control.
a: Phone to gateway: spoofing (authenticity), using stolen credentials. Control: MFA and device binding. Gateway to transfer service: tampering (integrity), by altering the amount or payee in transit. Control: TLS on each hop plus signed transfer requests, which also give non-repudiation. Transfer service to core banking: elevation of privilege (authorisation), through an over-privileged service account. Control: least privilege and authorising each operation. Across all three, protected audit logs counter repudiation.

q: A bank's control list for online banking is: TLS, a web application firewall, MFA, a password policy and data-centre locks. An auditor calls it unbalanced. Classify the controls, find the gaps and fill them.
a: TLS, the web application firewall and MFA are technical and preventive. The password policy is administrative and preventive. The locks are physical and preventive. Everything prevents; nothing detects or corrects. Add detective controls (an IDS, log review, CCTV in the data centre) and corrective ones (tested backups, incident response, access revocation). Check every major risk against a grid of type (technical, administrative, physical) by category (preventive, detective, corrective).

q: Design how a web login protects a password from browser to the final consumer, when TLS terminates at a DMZ proxy. Discuss the limits of TLS.
a: TLS protects each connection between its own endpoints, so if it ends at the DMZ proxy, the password is plaintext there even if the next hop also uses TLS. To protect it through that intermediary, encrypt the password field for the final consumer with its public key, plus a nonce that is checked against replay. Protect that private key. Use authenticated ephemeral key agreement for forward secrecy on each connection. Any inspection proxy that decrypts traffic sees plaintext, so include it in the trust boundary.

q: A small company runs its app server and database on one flat network. The app server's account is a database superuser, admins use their everyday laptops to manage servers, and permissions are cached at login for a day. Apply the four secure design principles.
a: Defence in depth: add zones (DMZ, internal) with firewalls between them, encryption of sensitive data, and an IDS, so one breach doesn't expose everything. Least common mechanism: give administration and logging their own out-of-band network and dedicated admin devices, and use separate keys per purpose. Least privilege: the app server account gets only the table reads and writes it needs, never superuser. Complete mediation: check authorisation on every request instead of caching it for a day, so revocations take effect immediately. Each fix adds cost or latency, so prioritise them by the risks they reduce.

q: In a DMZ-based architecture, decide where you would use an IDS and where an IPS, and how you would handle false positives.
a: Put an inline IPS at the internet edge, where blocking obvious attacks is worth the occasional false block. Place NIDS sensors at internal zone boundaries, such as between the DMZ and the internal network, so they alert without blocking business traffic, and HIDS on critical hosts like the database, which encrypted traffic would otherwise hide. Tune signatures, start new rules in alert-only mode, and review alerts. A passive IDS sees copied traffic and cannot stop an attack, so pair it with a response process.

q: System A fails twice a year for 4 hours each time. System B fails every day for 3 seconds. Which is more available, which is more reliable, and which would you rather run a payment service on?
a: B is more available: about 18 minutes down per year (99.997%) against A's 8 hours (99.91%). A is more reliable: it runs much longer between failures. For payments, B's daily failures could break transactions in progress, so choose by which failure the service tolerates. High availability does not imply high reliability.

q: A service is agreed to run 7 am to 7 pm on 22 working days a month. This month it was down for 2 hours at 3 am and 1 hour at noon. What is its availability?
a: AST = 12 x 22 = 264 hours. Only the noon outage falls inside the agreed service time, so DT = 1 hour, and availability = (264 - 1) / 264 = 99.62%. The 3 am outage does not count against this measure, which is why the agreed service time must be stated with any availability figure.

q: A service has MTTF of 999 hours and MTTR of 1 hour. You can either halve how often it fails or halve its recovery time. Which raises availability more?
a: Both give about the same result: 1998 / 1999 and 999 / 999.5 are both about 99.95%, up from 99.9%, because each halves the share of time spent recovering. Choose by cost and side effects: fewer failures also improves reliability, while faster recovery (monitoring, automated failover) is often cheaper to achieve.

q: A chain has a CDN at 99.99%, a web server pair at 99.99%, a single application server at 99% and a database pair at 99.99%. The budget covers one improvement: upgrade the CDN to 99.999%, or add a second application server. Which?
a: Add the application server. Now the chain is 0.9999^3 x 0.99, about 98.97%. A second application server makes that tier 99.99%, giving about 99.96%. The CDN upgrade gives only about 98.98%. In series the weakest component dominates. This assumes independent failures and enough capacity in the surviving server.

q: A teammate says two 99% servers in parallel give 99.99%, so the service now meets four nines. What must be true for that claim to hold?
a: Failures must be independent, failover must work and be fast, and either server must be able to carry the full load alone. The rest of the request path must also reach four nines, because everything in series multiplies. Shared power, storage or a common software bug break the independence assumption and make 99.99% optimistic.

q: Two replicas share one power supply. Can you apply the independent parallel formula to the whole service?
a: Not without modelling the common dependency. Both replicas can fail together when power fails; put the required power supply in series with the replica group, or remove that shared failure domain.

q: An SLA promises 99.99% availability per year, and planned downtime counts. A database upgrade needs 2 hours offline. Can you do it without breaching the SLA?
a: No. 99.99% allows (1 - 0.9999) x 525,600 = 52.56 minutes of downtime a year, and 2 hours alone exceeds that. Either do the upgrade without downtime (a rolling upgrade across redundant nodes) or agree a maintenance window outside the agreed service time. At 99.9% (8.76 hours a year), the 2-hour upgrade would fit.

q: Leadership wants every system in the company engineered for 99.99% availability. Critique the directive.
a: Each extra nine and each redundant component costs more, so apply it by criticality. Classify functions as critical or non-critical, give the critical ones redundancy and the higher target, and accept lower targets elsewhere. The architect's job is to meet the required availability at acceptable cost, not to maximise it everywhere.

q: After load shedding is enabled at 80% CPU, incoming traffic to a service doubles within a minute. What is happening, and what is the fix?
a: Retry spikes: rejected clients retry immediately, adding load to a service that is already overloaded. Add a retry policy (limits and backoff on clients) alongside the shedding threshold, plus per-user rate limits for greedy clients. Shedding without retry control can make overload worse.

q: Last year's 14 hours of downtime came mostly from the monthly release process. What kind of downtime is this, and what would you change?
a: Release windows are planned downtime, which continuous delivery and deployment reduce. Failed releases cause unplanned downtime, which phased rollouts and systematic rollback reduce. Changing the release process is likely to cut more downtime than adding hardware redundancy, which does not fix bad deployments.
