q: One API client's nightly batch job floods a shared service and slows everyone else down. Which cloud-level cause is this, and how would you fix it?
a: A noisy neighbour. Enforce rate limits per user or API key (or per IP address), sized so normal clients are unaffected. The cost is that the batch client must spread its load or negotiate a higher quota.

q: Behind a load balancer, instance 1 crashes, then instance 2 crashes 20 minutes later, then the rest go within 10 minutes. What is the likely cause, and how would you confirm it?
a: A chain reaction: all instances run the same logic, so a bug such as a memory leak triggered by a particular operation kills the busiest instance first. The survivors take its load and fail faster. Confirm by checking memory growth and the request mix on each instance before it crashed. Adding instances only delays the collapse; fix or isolate the triggering operation.

q: For a marketing campaign the front end scales from 6 to 75 instances (3,000 threads), while the back end stays at 6 instances with 450 threads. What fails first, and what would you change?
a: The back end: it has many fan-ins and bounded capacity, and now receives far more concurrent calls than its 450 threads can serve. Requests queue, time out and trigger retries. Scale the back end in step or cap calls with backpressure or rate limits, and load-test with the scaled-out front end.

q: After a full restart, the database hits 100% CPU and the system takes 40 minutes to recover, although normal load is 30% CPU. Diagnose it and suggest a fix.
a: A dogpile: every service tries to warm its in-memory cache from the database at the same moment, just as the database is recovering. Bring services back gradually rather than all at once, and limit the rate of cache-fill queries so the database is not swamped.

q: A user with 30 million followers posts, and the notification service falls an hour behind. Which failure source is this, and what would you consider?
a: A heavy operation from a special user: one action fans out to millions of deliveries. Handle such accounts differently, for example by fetching their posts when followers read rather than pushing to every follower, and isolate their processing so it cannot starve normal users.

q: A product page calls a recommendations service that sometimes hangs for 30 s. Design the protection: timeout, circuit-breaker behaviour and fallback.
a: Set a short timeout, well below the page's response target, with at most one retry. Wrap the call in a circuit breaker that opens after repeated failures and fails fast, then tests the service with trial calls while half-open, closing again on success. The fallback is a generic list such as best-sellers. Log state changes for operators. Customers see less personalised pages while the breaker is open.

q: Payments and report generation share one database connection pool of 50. A slow report query exhausts the pool, and payments fail. What would you change?
a: Apply a bulkhead: give payments and reports separate connection pools, or separate instances, so a report cannot exhaust the resources payments need. The cost is less efficient sharing: one pool may sit idle while the other waits.

q: A fault tree for 'checkout unavailable' has minimal cut sets {DNS failure}, {primary database fails AND replica fails} and {payment gateway down}. Where do you focus first?
a: On the singletons, DNS and the payment gateway: each alone takes checkout down. Add redundant DNS, and a second gateway or a degraded mode such as holding orders for later payment. The database needs two failures together, so it is already protected, provided the primary and replica really fail independently.

q: A team wants to start chaos engineering by randomly killing production database nodes next week. Critique the plan.
a: Start with the prerequisites: tracing and monitoring that show the agreed service outcome, and a stated hypothesis ('losing one replica does not raise checkout errors'). Then inject a targeted, contained fault, analyse the result, and only then automate and repeat. Random destruction without monitoring and a hypothesis teaches nothing and risks real outages.

q: A booking service keeps user sessions in local memory and must survive one server failure. Active/passive or active/active?
a: Active/active spreads load across live servers and survives one loss only if sessions are moved out of local memory into a shared store. Active/passive is simpler, but sessions are lost at failover unless they are replicated, and the standby sits idle. In both, a floating IP moves the address, not the state. If you can externalise the sessions, active/active gives more capacity.

q: You have four 3 TB disks, must survive any two disk failures, and need at least 6 TB usable. Which RAID level, and why not RAID 10?
a: RAID 6: two disks' worth of parity gives 6 TB usable and survives any two failures. RAID 10 also gives 6 TB but guarantees only one failure; two failures in the same mirror lose data. RAID 6 pays for this with parity overhead on writes.

q: Two disks fail in a four-disk RAID 10 array. Is the data necessarily lost?
a: It depends on placement. One failure in each mirror leaves a working copy; both failures in the same mirror lose that stripe's copies. A failure count alone is insufficient.

q: A team says: 'We have a backup server with nightly copies of all files, so we have server redundancy.' Do you agree?
a: No. A backup server supports recovery; it does not provide live compute failover. If the main server fails, the service is down until a restore and rebuild finish, so recovery time is long and up to a day of changes is lost. Server redundancy needs a prepared standby or active peers with current state.

q: A full backup runs Sunday night and incrementals run Monday to Friday nights. The disk fails on Saturday afternoon. What must you restore, and how would differential backups compare?
a: With incrementals, restore Sunday's full and then all five incrementals (Monday to Friday) in order; losing any one breaks the chain. With differentials, restore Sunday's full and only Friday's differential, which is simpler and faster. Either way, Saturday's changes since Friday night are lost.

q: A full backup takes 6 hours, the nightly window is 2 hours, and a full restore must finish within 4 hours. Which backup scheme fits?
a: A nightly full backup doesn't fit the window. Take the full backup at the weekend and differentials on weeknights: each differential is smaller than a full, and a restore needs only two sets. Check that late-week differentials still fit the 2-hour window and that full plus differential restores within 4 hours. Incrementals fit the window best but make restores slower and more fragile.

q: A manager wants to remove the standby database because 'we already take hourly incremental backups'. Do you agree?
a: No. Backups are a recovery measure that affects MTTR, not live redundancy. A restore from a full plus many incrementals takes hours and loses up to an hour of data, while a standby takes over in minutes. Keep both, or accept the much longer outage explicitly.

q: A design has two load-balanced web servers behind one load balancer, with one database and one shared file system. Where are the single points of failure?
a: The load balancer (fix it with a hot standby), the database, the shared file system, and any single firewall or network link on the path. Redundancy at the web tier does not make the whole service redundant. Check every required dependency.

q: The requirement is to survive the loss of an entire data centre and recover within 5 minutes. The current design is a high-availability topology at one site. What must change?
a: Add wide area load balancing across a second site that has its own firewalls, load balancers, web servers, database and file system, with data replicated between the sites. This removes the single-site failure domain, at roughly double the infrastructure cost plus the complexity of cross-site data replication.

q: An internal HR tool needs 99% availability, and a payments API needs 99.99%. Which availability patterns would you pick for each?
a: HR: a basic or load-balanced web application is likely enough, since 99% allows about 3.65 days of downtime a year. Payments: a full high-availability topology with redundant load balancers, clusters and data tier, and possibly a second site, with end-to-end availability calculated and failover tested. Each step up costs more, so match the pattern to the required nines.

q: A team says Kubernetes will make their single-instance database highly available because it restarts failed pods. Do you agree?
a: Only partly. Restarting or rescheduling the pod shortens recovery, but the database is still down while it restarts, and a restart does not give the data a redundant copy. A node or storage failure can still lose service or data. Add replication across nodes, or a managed redundant database, and test recovery.

q: A two-node active/passive database cluster uses one shared storage array, and the array fails. What happens, and what alternative avoids it?
a: Both nodes lose the data, because shared disk delegates redundancy to the storage and the array is a single point of failure. A shared-nothing design, where each node owns its storage and data is replicated, avoids that, at the cost of managing replication and promotion.

q: A primary/replica database loses its primary at peak time. What happens to reads and writes, and what does recovery involve?
a: Reads can continue on the replica, but writes stop until a replica is promoted to primary, because only the primary accepts writes. Promotion takes time, and writes not yet replicated may be lost. Read replicas provide read capacity and redundancy, not independent write leaders.

q: Application instances are spread across two availability zones, but the database runs in one zone and is protected by periodic snapshots. That zone fails. What happens?
a: The compute survives, but the service loses its data tier. Restoring from a snapshot takes time and loses every change since the snapshot. Spreading compute alone is not enough: replicate the database across zones, or plan an explicit data recovery that meets the recovery target.

q: A web system has an active/passive load balancer pair (99% each), two web servers in parallel (99% each), one application server (99%), an active/passive database pair (99% each) and one firewall (98%). The target is 99.9%. Calculate end-to-end availability, say whether it meets the target, and recommend improvements with their assumptions.
a: Each pair gives 1 - 0.01^2 = 0.9999. In series: 0.9999^3 x 0.99 x 0.98 = 96.99%, which misses 99.9% badly because of the single application server and firewall. Replicating both gives 0.9999^4 x (1 - 0.02^2) = 99.92%, which just meets the target. This assumes independent failures, working failover and enough capacity in the survivors. Shared power, storage or a common software fault would lower the real figure, so test failover and check for shared failure domains.

q: A monthly SLA promises 99.95% over a 30-day, 24-hour service month. This month had a 15-minute unplanned outage and a 20-minute planned maintenance window. Does the service meet the SLA? What changes the answer, and what would you change in the design?
a: The month has 43,200 minutes, so 99.95% allows 21.6 minutes of downtime. The outage alone is 15 minutes (99.965%), which passes. If planned maintenance counts, the total is 35 minutes (99.919%), which fails. The answer depends on whether the agreed service time excludes the maintenance window. Design changes: rolling or blue/green deployments, so maintenance needs no downtime, and faster detection and failover to shorten unplanned outages.

q: Service A receives 100 requests/s and has 200 worker threads. Each request calls service B with a 30 s timeout. B slows from 50 ms to 10 s per call. Explain what happens to A, and design the containment.
a: By Little's Law, A needs 100 x 10 = 1,000 requests in flight but has 200 threads, so the pool is exhausted within about 2 seconds. A stops responding and its own callers fail: a cascading failure, made worse by retries. Containment: a short timeout (1 s would keep about 100 requests in flight), a circuit breaker that fails fast with a fallback once B is unhealthy, a bulkhead so calls to B use their own limited pool and cannot take every thread, and bounded retries with backoff. Validate it by injecting latency into B in a chaos experiment.

q: An e-commerce site needs 99.99% availability for checkout. The data tier is the weak point. Compare two database redundancy models and recommend one, stating what you would monitor.
a: Active/passive with shared disk is simple failover, but the shared storage is a single point of failure unless the array itself is redundant. Shared-nothing replication (a primary with replicas, or multi-node replication) gives each node its own storage, avoiding that, but needs promotion rules and risks losing unreplicated writes at failover. For 99.99%, prefer shared-nothing replication across failure domains, with automated, tested promotion and enough capacity in the survivors, plus RAID and tested backups for recovery. Monitor replication lag, failover time and data loss in failover tests, and calculate end-to-end availability rather than trusting the topology label.

q: A database holds 2 TB. A full backup takes 5 hours, the nightly window is 2 hours, daily changes are about 50 GB, and the recovery-time target is 3 hours. Compare full, differential and incremental backup and recommend a scheme.
a: A nightly full backup is impossible (5 hours against a 2-hour window). Weekly full plus nightly incrementals copies only about 50 GB a night, but a restore late in the week needs the full plus up to six incrementals in order, which is the slowest and most fragile option. Weekly full plus nightly differentials grows to about 300 GB by day six, which must still fit the window, and a restore needs only the full plus one differential. Recommend the differential scheme if day-six differentials fit the window. Then test whether a 2 TB full restore can finish within 3 hours. If it cannot, backups alone cannot meet the target, and you need a standby replica.

q: Choose a RAID level for an array of four 3 TB disks that must tolerate any two simultaneous disk failures, and state its cost against the alternatives.
a: RAID 6 guarantees any two disk failures with at least four disks. Two disks' worth of capacity holds parity, so four 3 TB disks provide 6 TB usable. Parity updates add write overhead, and actual speed depends on workload and implementation. RAID 10 gives the same 6 TB but guarantees only one failure (two only if they are in different mirrors). RAID 5 gives 9 TB with one-failure tolerance, and RAID 0 has no protection.

q: A vendor offers a server with a 30% faster CPU clock. Your application spends 70% of each request waiting on the database. Will throughput rise by 30%?
a: No. Throughput reflects the whole system, and here the database dominates, so a faster CPU speeds up only the small CPU share of the work. Measure throughput under your own workload before paying for clock speed. Upgrading the bottleneck resource (the database, or how it is used) is what raises throughput.

q: A dashboard shows CPU at 20%, and the team concludes performance is fine. Users report 8-second responses. What is wrong with the conclusion?
a: Low utilisation is not proof of good performance. The time may be spent waiting on another resource (database locks, disk, a slow dependency, the network), or the CPU may be idle because work is stuck elsewhere. Look at response time, throughput and the utilisation of each resource together to find where the time goes.

q: A load test fires requests back-to-back from 500 virtual users with zero think time. Real users pause about 10 s between actions, and responses take about 1 s. What does the test misrepresent?
a: The load. With no think time, 500 users generate about 500 requests/s; with a 10 s pause they generate about 500 / (10 + 1), roughly 45 requests/s. The test therefore models a far heavier load than 500 real users. Set realistic think times and arrival rates, or the results won't map to the requirement.

q: Average response time rose from 300 ms to 2 s while service time stayed at 250 ms. Where did the extra time go, and how would you confirm it?
a: Response time is service time plus waiting time plus transmission time. With service unchanged, the growth is almost certainly waiting in queues caused by higher utilisation, or possibly transmission. Confirm by checking queue lengths, utilisation and network timings at each tier.

q: Three tiers in series take 50, 100 and 600 ms per request and have capacities of 40, 12 and 25 requests/s. Which tier do you work on to cut response time, and which to raise throughput?
a: For response time, the 600 ms tier, which is the largest share of the 750 ms total. For throughput, the 12 requests/s tier, which caps the pipeline. They are different tiers: the biggest contributor to response time is not necessarily the capacity bottleneck, so measure both.

q: Four tiers have throughputs 10, 16, 6 and 20 tps in series. What is system throughput, and what happens if you double the DB?
a: System throughput is min = 6 tps (app server). Doubling the DB changes nothing because the app server remains the bottleneck.

q: A system can complete at most 20 requests/s and receives 22/s for an hour. What happens to throughput and response time?
a: Throughput stays at 20/s, its capacity. The excess 2 requests/s either queue or are rejected. With an unbounded queue, about 7,200 requests are waiting after an hour, and response time keeps climbing with no steady state. Add capacity or shed or throttle load; waiting it out does not help.

q: A page calls three services in parallel, taking 120, 300 and 80 ms, and needs all three results. A teammate estimates 500 ms for the page. Do you agree?
a: No. Branches that run concurrently contribute their maximum, so the page takes about 300 ms plus coordination overhead. The 300 ms service is the one to speed up; improving the other two changes nothing. If the calls were sequential, the teammate's sum would be right.

q: Each request uses 40 ms of application CPU and makes 3 database calls of 20 ms each. At 15 requests/s, which resource saturates first, and at what request rate?
a: Service demand: CPU 40 ms, database 3 x 20 = 60 ms. At 15 requests/s, the database is 15 x 0.06 = 90% busy and the CPU 60%. The database saturates first, at 1 / 0.06, about 16.7 requests/s. Cutting database visits per request (for example by batching or caching) raises that limit more than a faster CPU would.

q: A gateway forwards 125 packets/s, taking 2 ms each. What is its utilisation, and at what rate does it saturate?
a: U = 125 x 0.002 = 25%. It saturates at 1 / 0.002 = 500 packets/s. Response time will rise sharply well before that point because of queueing, so don't plan to run it near 100%.

q: A colleague says you cannot apply the Utilization Law because the arrivals are bursty, not Poisson. Do you agree?
a: No. The operational laws are identities over measured quantities: U = XS holds for the observed interval, whatever the arrival distribution. What does need distribution assumptions is predicting queueing delay, as in M/M/1. Keep the units, interval and system boundary consistent.

q: A server has a pool of 40 threads. Requests arrive at 100/s and spend 0.3 s each in the server. Is the pool big enough, and what if a slow dependency raises the time to 0.6 s?
a: By Little's Law, n = 100 x 0.3 = 30 requests in the server, which fits within 40 threads. At 0.6 s, n = 60, more than the pool: requests queue for threads, response time climbs further, and the failure can cascade upstream. A timeout on the dependency, or a larger pool, protects against this.

q: Measured per-visit response times: CPU 0.25 s over 181 visits, storage A 0.203 s over 80 visits, storage B 0.071 s over 100 visits. Which contributes most to the 68.6 s job time, and what does that suggest?
a: By the General Response Time Law: CPU 0.25 x 181, about 45.3 s; A 0.203 x 80, about 16.2 s; B 0.071 x 100, about 7.1 s. The CPU dominates, mostly because of its visit count. Reduce the CPU's visits or its per-visit time before tuning storage.

q: A shop serves 15 customers an hour, and you observe an average of 3 customers inside. How long does a customer spend in the shop?
a: R = n / λ = 3 / 0.25 per minute = 12 minutes. That includes both waiting and service, because n counted everyone inside. Use the same boundary for n and R.

q: Orders arrive at 20 an hour, and one server completes 30 an hour, giving a 6-minute average time in system. The target is under 3 minutes. Would a server that completes 45 an hour meet it?
a: Yes. Under M/M/1, R = 1 / (µ - λ) = 1 / (45 - 20) hours = 2.4 minutes. Utilisation falls from 67% to 44%, which is where the waiting time goes. This assumes random (Poisson) arrivals and exponential service, so validate with measured data.

q: Average utilization is 75%, so why is there still a queue?
a: Arrivals are random and bursty. A burst of jobs arrives faster than the server can handle even though the average load is below capacity, so waiting occurs; response time rises as 1/(1 - U).

q: To save money, a team plans to run its application servers at 90% CPU. Service time is 1 s, and the response target is 3 s. Under M/M/1, is the plan safe?
a: No. R = S / (1 - U) gives 10 s at 90%, far over target. Meeting 3 s needs U of 2/3 or less (1 / (1 - 0.67) = 3). Size the headroom from the response target and measured workload; there is no universally safe percentage.

q: Arrivals and service capacity are both 30 requests/hour. Can M/M/1 predict a finite mean response time?
a: No. U = 1, so the steady-state denominator µ - λ is zero. The model requires λ < µ; equality leaves no spare capacity to drain random bursts.

q: A bank branch has 4 tellers. Should each teller have their own line, or should one shared line feed all four?
a: One shared line. With identical tellers, a free teller always takes the next customer, whereas separate lines can leave one teller idle while another line waits. This assumes every teller can serve every customer; specialised counters change the comparison.

q: You need to triple capacity: one server three times faster, or three servers? Give the performance answer and the availability answer.
a: For response time, the lecture's ideal model favours one fast server, then three servers sharing a queue, then three separate queues. For availability, the single fast server is a single point of failure, while three servers survive one loss. Most production systems accept slightly higher response time for that redundancy.

q: A sizing target says 'queueing below 3 minutes', and service takes 1.5 minutes. What response-time limit should you test?
a: R = waiting + service, so require R < 4.5 minutes. Comparing a response-time formula directly with 3 minutes would impose a different, stricter target.

q: Server A costs $10,000 and delivers 500 tps. Server B costs $3,000 and delivers 120 tps. Which has better price/performance, and what else would you check?
a: A: $20 per tps; B: $25 per tps, so A is better on capital cost. Also check operating costs and expected lifetime (Google counted both when choosing commodity servers), the impact of losing one large server versus one small one, and whether the load comes in steps that suit smaller units.

q: Adding a second server behind a load balancer halved average response time, although each request's processing time did not change. Why?
a: Each server's utilisation roughly halved, so requests spend far less time waiting in queues; response time is waiting plus service. The service time is unchanged. To cut it, you would need faster processing or parallel work within the request itself.

q: A load balancer uses least-connections with sticky sessions. After a campaign, one server holds 60% of active users and is overloaded. Diagnose it and fix it.
a: Stickiness overrides the balancing policy: users stay pinned to the server that first held their session. Move session state out of the servers into a shared store so any server can take any request. The cost is a network hop to the state store.

q: A partner's month-end batch job floods the system with requests, and interactive users time out. Which tactic family applies, and what would you do?
a: Control resource demand: manage the arrival rate (throttle the partner) and prioritise input, so interactive requests go ahead of batch. The batch job takes longer as a result. Adding resources would also work, but costs more for a predictable monthly peak.

q: Servers of different sizes (8 and 32 cores) sit behind a round-robin load balancer, and the small ones are overloaded. What would you change?
a: Round robin ignores capability, so the 8-core servers get the same share as the 32-core ones. Use a capability-weighted or server-load policy, or least response time, so work follows actual capacity.

q: Cache access takes 8 ms, the source takes 50 ms, and the hit ratio is 20%. Is the cache worth it? If cache access were 15 ms, what hit ratio would you need?
a: At 8 ms: 0.2 x 8 + 0.8 x (8 + 50) = 48 ms against 50 ms without the cache, a small gain. At 15 ms, the expected time is 15 + (1 - h) x 50, which must be under 50, so h must exceed 30%. Below that, the cache adds cost and latency.

q: A social app's feed reads outnumber posts 50 to 1, and one account has 20 million followers. Fan-out on write, fan-out on read, or a hybrid?
a: A hybrid. Fan-out on write precomputes timelines, so the dominant reads are cheap. For the 20-million-follower account, writing to every follower's timeline on each post is too costly, so merge its posts in at read time. The trade-off is extra read-time work for followers of such accounts, as in the lecture's Twitter example.

q: With 15 GB of cache and data types A (10 GB, 10 ms), B (20 GB, 30 ms), C (30 GB, 10 ms), what do you cache?
a: The full-cache average benefit/GB ranks B, A, C, but B needs 20 GB for its measured 30 ms gain. With only 15 GB, measure partial hit ratios and marginal benefits, then allocate the available space. The full-cache ratios alone do not prove the best split.

q: A product catalogue has 1 million items. In shop X, access is spread evenly across them; in shop Y, it follows a power law. A cache holds 1% of the items. Where does it help?
a: In shop Y: under a power law, a small set of popular items gets most of the requests, so 1% of items can yield a high hit ratio. In shop X, access is uniform, so a 1% cache gives roughly a 1% hit ratio, which is not worth it. Measure the access distribution before sizing a cache.

q: A matching job takes 2 s for 10,000 candidates using an O(n^2) algorithm. Data will grow to 100,000. Would you buy 10x hardware or change the algorithm?
a: O(n^2) means 100 times the work, about 200 s. Even with 10x hardware that scales perfectly, it still takes about 20 s, and every further growth repeats the problem. An O(n log n) algorithm grows only about 12.5 times for 10 times the data. Change the algorithm, and verify with measurements at the expected size, because constants and I/O also matter.

q: Scoring every candidate-job pair currently happens in the application server, which pulls all the rows over the network to return the top 1,000. When should the scoring move into the database server?
a: When the data volume is large and the result small, as here: running it in the database transfers only 1,000 results instead of every row. The trade-off is load on the database server, which is usually harder to scale, so check its spare capacity first.

q: A 'friends of friends within 3 hops' query on a relational store takes 9 seconds. What would you investigate?
a: The data store, which is often the bottleneck: first the indexes on the relationship tables, then whether the storage technology fits. Relationship-heavy traversals like this suit a graph database. Switching stores is costly, so prove the gain with a prototype first.

q: One API customer sends 25 large requests at once, and everyone else's requests wait behind them. What would you add?
a: Flow control: per-client rate limits, plus fair queueing or separate lanes, so one demanding client or burst cannot starve the others. That customer's batch then takes longer, which you can offer as a paid higher limit if it matters.

q: A team will adopt a message broker none of them has used, with a target of 2,000 messages/s at peak. What would you do before the full build?
a: Prototype and benchmark it: set the goal (2,000 messages/s at the required latency), decide how much to build, instrument it, run it at the target load, and repeat until the risk is contained. Unknown technology is exactly where you should fail early. The trade-off is confidence against prototyping effort.

q: Two developers time the search API from home with a browser tool and get 0.8 s and 4 s. Why are the results unreliable, and how would you test properly?
a: The client, network and load are uncontrolled, and each person sends a handful of requests, so the numbers reflect their connections, not the system under its required load. Use a scripted load test from a controlled environment, with a defined arrival rate, think time and request mix, and report percentiles against the target. A queueing model or simulation can complement it.

q: A performance document shows only one box diagram: front end, service layer, back ends. What is missing?
a: The performance-relevant detail: a sequence diagram showing call order and loops, such as repeated back-end calls per request, and a data flow showing large messages, calls that carry many records, and high-frequency interactions. Aim for the level of detail where these become visible, without drawing every class.

q: A request passes a firewall (5 ms wait, 45 ms service, 10 tps capacity), a reverse proxy (10, 90, 16 tps), an app server (50, 550, 6 tps) and a database (30, 300, 20 tps), with 200 ms of network latency. (a) Find the response time and throughput. (b) You add a second app server. What is the new throughput, and what is the next bottleneck?
a: (a) Response time = 50 + 100 + 600 + 330 = 1080 ms, plus 200 ms latency, giving 1280 ms. Throughput = min(10, 16, 6, 20) = 6 tps, limited by the app server. (b) Two app servers give about 12 tps, so throughput becomes min(10, 16, 12, 20) = 10 tps, and the firewall is now the bottleneck. Each request's service time is unchanged, so response time improves only through less queueing at the app tier. To go beyond 10 tps, scale the firewall as well.

q: Each job needs 5 s of CPU, 80 I/Os on storage A (50 ms each) and 100 I/Os on storage B (30 ms each). Storage A is observed at 15.70 I/Os per second. Find the system throughput, the utilisations and the bottleneck. What would it take to double throughput?
a: Forced Flow: λ_0 = 15.70 / 80 = 0.196 jobs/s. Demands: CPU 5 s, A 4 s, B 3 s. U = λ_0 x D gives CPU 98%, A 78.4%, B 58.8%; the CPU is the bottleneck, and maximum throughput is 1 / 5 = 0.2 jobs/s. To double to about 0.39 jobs/s, every demand must fall below about 2.56 s. Halving CPU demand alone leaves A as the limit at 1 / 4 = 0.25 jobs/s, so storage A, and storage B (3 s), also need faster devices, fewer visits or more parallel units. Bottlenecks move as you fix them.

q: A shop receives 20 requests an hour, and one server handles 30 an hour. Compute the utilisation and average time in system. Then, at 2 requests per minute with a 1.5-minute service time and a target of queueing under 3 minutes, a faster server is not possible: how many servers do you need with separate queues, and with one shared queue?
a: For 20/hour arrivals and 30/hour capacity, U = 2/3 and R = 6 minutes including service. For λ = 2/min and S = 1.5 minutes, the offered load is 3, so ρ = 3/c. Waiting under 3 minutes means R < 4.5. Separate queues need c = 5; the lecture's approximate shared-queue model gives c = 4. Both need ρ < 1. Validate the chosen model with measured data and add headroom for a server failure.

q: 1000 players each trigger an event every 3 s (think time). Server time is 50 ms and the round trip is 200 ms. What load must the server handle, and how many requests are in flight?
a: Assuming one outstanding request per player and no queueing, the rate is 1000 / (3 + 0.05 + 0.2) = 307.7/s. Work in the server averages 307.7 x 0.05 = 15.4 requests. Including network time, 307.7 x 0.25 = 76.9 requests are in flight. State the boundary you are counting; the remaining players are thinking.

q: A product-detail lookup takes 50 ms from the database. A cache would take 5 ms. Measured access is uniform across the catalogue, and a cache the size you can afford gives a 20% hit ratio. A teammate says to add the cache. Argue for or against, and say what would change your mind.
a: Expected time = 0.2 x 5 + 0.8 x 55 = 45 ms against 50 ms: a 10% gain for the cost of the cache memory and an extra component, which is weak. It stops paying at all if cache access reaches 10 ms or the hit ratio falls. With uniform access, a larger cache raises hits only in proportion to its size. What would change the decision: a power-law access pattern, where a small cache catches most requests; precomputing the expensive part of the page; or a source that is much slower than 50 ms. Measure before buying.

q: A web tier runs at 85% utilisation with 4 s average response time against a 2 s target, and 40% of requests fetch the same home-page data. Which tactics would you apply, in what order, and how would you verify them before building?
a: First reduce demand: cache or precompute the home-page data, removing up to 40% of the work and lowering utilisation and queueing. Then manage resources: add servers behind a load balancer (shared queue) so per-server utilisation falls well below 85%, and fix any algorithmic or database bottleneck the measurements show. If needed, throttle or deprioritise non-interactive load. Verify with a queueing model or simulation (for example JMT) and an instrumented prototype benchmark under the real request mix, repeating until the 2 s target holds with headroom.

q: A photo app expects 50,000 uploads a day at an average of 3 MB, and keeps 3 copies of each photo. Apply the capacity-planning model to estimate storage growth.
a: Forecast workload: 50,000 uploads a day. Workload-to-resource relationship: 3 MB x 3 copies = 9 MB per upload. Derived capacity: about 450 GB a day (decimal units), or roughly 164 TB a year, plus indexes, logs, overhead and headroom. Each input is an assumption to monitor: if the upload rate or photo size grows, the estimate scales with it.

q: CPU graphs have risen steadily for months. The business asks what happens if sign-ups double. Can you answer from the system metrics alone?
a: No. CPU shows the symptom, not the driver. You need application-level metrics (sign-ups, uploads, API calls per key) and how each relates to resource use, so you can turn a business forecast into a resource forecast. Start collecting them alongside the system metrics, and fit the relationship from history.

q: A new system has no production data yet, and the vendor publishes a benchmark for similar hardware. Which data source would you use, and what is the risk?
a: Use the vendor benchmark as a starting point, and self-benchmark the significant scenarios if you can. The risk is that the vendor's workload and configuration differ from yours, so its numbers may not transfer. Once the system runs, switch to monitoring data, which is the best source.

q: An application writes 20 GB of logs a day and must keep them for 90 days. The busiest day so far produced 35 GB. How much log storage do you plan for?
a: Disk is cumulative: plan for everything retained over 90 days, not the peak day. At the average, 20 x 90 = 1.8 TB. Since some days reach 35 GB, add headroom or forecast growth in the daily rate, plus overhead for indexes and any replicas.

q: Transactions start at 1M a month and grow 10% a month, with 24-month retention and 1 MB per record. A teammate estimates 24 x 1M x 1 MB = 24 TB. Do you agree?
a: No. That ignores growth. Monthly volume is a geometric series: 1M x (1.1^24 - 1) / 0.1, about 88.5M transactions, or about 88.5 TB, so the teammate's figure is less than a third of the need. Add fixed overhead, indexes and replicas, and revisit the forecast as actual growth is observed.

q: After two years, does 24-month retention mean a growing system's storage stops growing?
a: Not necessarily. Old records expire, but newer months may contain more records than the months removed. Forecast the sum within the moving 24-month window using the expected arrival growth.

q: Your 88.5 TB data estimate covers records only. The database adds indexes of about 30% of data size and keeps one full replica. What is the real storage need?
a: 88.5 x 1.3 for indexes is about 115 TB; doubled for the replica, about 230 TB, plus the fixed OS and database baseline and a buffer. Size data feeds and overheads separately and state the assumptions, so each can be revised.

q: Storage use rises steadily month by month. A different metric, order volume, spikes every December. Which forecasting approach suits each?
a: Storage is trending, so fit a regression (linear or exponential) and extrapolate. Orders are seasonal, so model the yearly cycle explicitly, for example by comparing each December with previous ones. A simple moving average or exponential smoothing would smooth out the December spike rather than predict it.

q: After a merger, traffic stepped up permanently by 40%. Your exponential-smoothing forecast with alpha = 0.1 still lags far behind. Why, and what would you change?
a: A low alpha gives little weight to the latest observation, so the forecast adjusts slowly to a real level change. Raise alpha so it reacts faster, or refit from the post-merger data. A high alpha also chases noise, so choose it for how quickly real change happens.

q: A linear fit says the disk fills on day 70 and an exponential fit says day 55. Today is day 20, and procurement takes 7 weeks. When do you order?
a: Now. Seven weeks is 49 days. The linear forecast leaves 50 days, with almost no margin, and the exponential one leaves 35, which is already too late. Both are extrapolations with error, so plan on the earlier date plus a buffer, and keep comparing the fits with new readings.

q: A service averages 200 requests/s, peaks at 900 requests/s on Monday mornings, and its data grows by 5 GB a day. How do you size the servers and the disk?
a: Servers are peak-driven: size for 900 requests/s at the response target, plus headroom for a node failure. Average load is irrelevant to that. Disk is cumulative: size for 5 GB a day over the retention period, plus overhead. Using the average for servers, or the peak for disk, would get both wrong.

q: The benchmark shows 17.04 tps on 1 machine, 30.81 on 2 and 55.76 on 4. A teammate plans 8 machines for 136 tps. Do you agree?
a: No. Each doubling has given about 1.8x, not 2x, so 8 machines might give about 101 tps if the trend holds, and it may get worse. The application servers' CPU was already at 95-98% at maximum load. Benchmark 8 machines, or fit a scalability model, before committing.

q: A reporting scenario is 4 times slower than the reference benchmark of 55.76 tps on 4 machines, and the business needs 30 report requests/s. Is 4 machines enough?
a: No. Estimated throughput is 55.76 / 4, about 13.9 tps, less than half the need. Adding machines will not scale linearly, so reduce the scenario's cost (precompute, cache, optimise queries) as well as adding capacity, and benchmark the actual report.

q: At maximum TPS, the application servers' CPU sits at 97% and the database server's at 2%. A teammate proposes a bigger database server. Respond.
a: Disagree. The application tier is the bottleneck, and the database is almost idle. A bigger database adds nothing until the application tier is scaled out or made cheaper per request. Re-measure afterwards, because the bottleneck may then move to the database.

q: A workload is 90% parallel. Going from 10 to 20 servers, how much speedup do you gain, and what is the ceiling?
a: Amdahl's law: S(10) = 1 / (0.1 + 0.09), about 5.26; S(20) = 1 / (0.1 + 0.045), about 6.90. Doubling the servers gives only about 31% more speedup, and the ceiling is 1 / (1 - 0.9) = 10, however many you add. Reducing the serial part pays more than adding servers.

q: Throughput rises up to 8 nodes, then falls at 12. Which model explains this, and what does it say about the cause?
a: USL, not Amdahl: Amdahl's speedup flattens but never falls. The decline comes from the crosstalk (coherency) term, kappa: nodes spend more and more effort coordinating with each other. Fit sigma and kappa to the measurements to find the peak, and reduce cross-node coordination if you need to scale further.

q: The parallel fraction P was measured with a load test that sent only login requests. Should you trust the resulting scaling prediction?
a: No. P depends on the workload mix: logins may parallelise well, while checkouts update shared data serially. An unrepresentative test gives the wrong P and the wrong server count. Repeat the test with a production-like mix.

q: Load tests show that a single shared stock-count row is updated on every order. How does that affect scaling, and what would you change?
a: Every order serialises on that row, which lowers the parallel fraction P and caps speedup at 1 / (1 - P). Reduce the serial part, for example by partitioning the stock count or updating it asynchronously, and accept the trade-off in exactness or consistency of the count.

q: With the lecture's mix, 4 machines give an estimated 38.8 tps. The forecast peak is 50 tps. How many machines would you plan for?
a: 50 / 38.8 is about 1.29 times the capacity, so a linear estimate says about 5.2 machines. Scaling has been sub-linear (about 1.8x per doubling), so plan to benchmark 6 or more with the production mix, then add headroom for a node failure. The weighted estimate is a simplified starting point, not deployable capacity.

q: If Payment's share rose from 5% to 10% (taking 5% from Login), what happens to overall throughput?
a: Within the lecture's weighted estimate, replacing 5% Login with Payment changes the total by 0.05 x (13.94 - 55.76) = -2.091 tps, giving about 36.7 tps. The actual production effect requires mixed-load measurement.

q: You have neither a reference benchmark nor a production system. How do you get sizing data?
a: Run simulated load tests (for example with JMeter or Artillery): define the scenarios, the mix and the arrival rates, then measure response time and throughput as load increases. Once a production system exists, switch to its monitoring data, which is the best source.

q: A team sized its servers from a one-hour sample taken on a Tuesday afternoon. What is the risk?
a: The sample hides daily and weekly cycles. If the real peak is Monday morning, as in the Flickr example, the servers will be undersized exactly when demand is highest. Measure over weeks, identify the recurring peak, and size for it.

q: A service used only in Asia expands to Europe. How might the load pattern change?
a: Time zones shift and blend the peaks: the European peak arrives hours after the Asian one, so the service is busy for more hours each day, and the peaks may overlap. Re-measure after the launch, and size for the combined peak, not either region alone.

q: Monday peak busy processes follow the trend y = 42.75x + 726, where x is weeks. Your servers handle 1,600 busy processes in total, and procurement takes 7 weeks. When do you run out, and when must you order?
a: Solve 42.75x + 726 = 1,600: x is about 20.4, so capacity runs out around week 20. With a 7-week lead time plus a buffer, order by about week 12 or 13. Check the trend against new weekly peaks, since a steeper trend moves the date earlier.

q: New instances take 5 minutes to start, and traffic doubles within 3 minutes at 9 am every weekday. How should the scaling work?
a: Reactive scaling will always be late, because demand doubles before new instances are ready. Use scheduled scaling from the historical pattern, adding capacity shortly before 9 am, and scale up aggressively for unexpected surges. Scale down conservatively afterwards, since briefly holding spare capacity costs little compared with failing users.

q: Two nodes handle 120 requests/s. Scale-out triggers above 55/node and scale-in below 45/node. Why might adding one node cause ping-pong?
a: Before scale-out each handles 60/s; after adding a third, each handles 40/s, below the 45/s scale-in threshold. Removing one returns to 60/s. Set thresholds and adjustments so the new state does not immediately trigger the opposite action; use cooldown as well.

q: The forecast says capacity runs out in 6 weeks. The procurement template totals about 7 weeks, plus 1 week to get downtime approved. What do you do now, and what do you change for next time?
a: You are already late for the normal process. Look for interim capacity (temporary cloud capacity, expedited delivery, or reducing or throttling demand), and start procurement immediately, running the downtime approval in parallel. Next time, trigger procurement from the forecast with the full lead time plus a buffer. Buying very early has its own cost, tying up money and missing price drops, so plan the date rather than stockpiling.

q: A database disk has 280 GB used of 500 GB, and the last 20 days of readings fit a linear trend of about 4.35 GB a day. Procurement takes about 7 weeks, plus 1 week for downtime approval. When does the disk fill, and when must you act? What could make the forecast wrong?
a: (500 - 280) / 4.35 is about 51 days, roughly 7 weeks, so the disk fills at about the point a normal 7-week procurement would deliver. With a buffer, and possibly the extra week for downtime approval, you must act now. What could go wrong: growth may be exponential rather than linear, which brings the date forward; logs and indexes may grow faster than the data; and 20 days of history is short. Compare linear and exponential fits, keep revising with new readings, and plan from the earlier date.

q: Estimate storage for 1 million transactions a month growing 10% a month, retained for 2 years, at 1 MB per record, with indexes adding 30% and one replica. Then explain what happens to storage in year 3.
a: The first 24 months hold 1M x (1.1^24 - 1) / 0.1, about 88.5M records, or 88.5 TB. With 30% for indexes that is about 115 TB, and with the replica about 230 TB, plus the fixed OS and database baseline and a buffer. In year 3, the oldest months expire, but each new month (about 9.8M records by month 25) is far larger than the month it replaces (1M), so storage keeps growing. Forecast the moving 24-month window, not a one-off total.

q: The 4-machine reference benchmark gives 55.76 tps. Slowness factors are Login 1.0, Search 2.0, Details 1.5, Cart 1.5, Checkout 2.0 and Payment 4.0, and the mix is 30/20/15/20/10/5%. The forecast peak is 45 tps, and the business wants to survive one machine failure. Estimate the capacity and recommend a machine count.
a: Weighted estimate: 16.73 + 5.58 + 5.58 + 7.43 + 2.79 + 0.70, about 38.8 tps on 4 machines, short of 45 tps. Scaling has been sub-linear (about 1.8x per doubling), so 45 tps needs more than a proportional 4.6 machines; and to survive one failure, the survivors must still deliver 45 tps. If the 1.8x-per-doubling trend holds, 5 machines give about 47 tps, so plan for 6 (5 survivors after a failure), and confirm it by benchmarking with the production mix. The estimate assumes uniform slowness across tiers and the benchmark's configuration, so validate it with a mixed load test.

q: Load tests measure 1,000 req/s on 1 node, 1,800 on 2, 3,000 on 4 and 3,200 on 8. Explain the pattern, estimate what 16 nodes would give, and recommend what to do.
a: Returns diminish quickly: 4 to 8 nodes adds only 7%. That suggests a large serial part (shared data, quotas) and possibly crosstalk. Amdahl caps speedup at 1 / (1 - P), and USL allows throughput to fall past a peak, so 16 nodes may give little or even less than 3,200 req/s. Fit USL's sigma and kappa to these points to find the peak, and don't buy 16 nodes without testing. Better value comes from reducing the serial work, such as shared-row updates or cross-node coordination, and rerunning the tests with a production-like mix.

q: Design an auto-scaling policy for a web tier with a Monday 9 am peak of 900 requests/s, nodes that handle 100 requests/s at the response target, and a 3-minute start-up time. Include thresholds that avoid ping-pong.
a: Use scheduled scaling from the weekly trend to reach about 10 nodes before 9 am: 9 for the load, plus 1 for headroom. React to surprises by scaling up aggressively, since start-up takes 3 minutes, and scale down conservatively with a cooldown. Thresholds, for example: scale out above 80 requests/s per node, scale in below 50. Check them: 4 nodes at 80 is 320 requests/s, which spread over 5 nodes gives 64, above the scale-in threshold; 5 nodes at 50 is 250, which over 4 nodes gives 62.5, below the scale-out threshold. So neither action immediately triggers the other. Revisit the thresholds as the Monday trend grows.

q: Two designs for a loyalty system: A ships in 2 months with the reward rules hard-coded; B takes 3 months with the rules isolated behind an interface and held in configuration. Marketing expects to change the rules monthly for 5 years. Which do you choose?
a: B. With about 60 rule changes expected, the extra month is repaid by cheaper, safer changes, and most lifecycle cost falls in maintenance (the lecture cites 80-90%). A would need a code change, test and release for every rule tweak. If the system were a short-lived campaign, A would be the better choice.

q: A team says it will 'make the code maintainable later, once we have users'. Do you agree?
a: Only partly. Detailed refactoring can wait, but boundaries, interfaces and variation points are architectural and cost far more to add once code depends on their absence. Put them where change is likely now, and defer the rest. How much to invest depends on the expected changes and the system's lifetime.

q: For an insurance product, actuaries change pricing factors monthly, and the screen layout changes about once a year. Which way of incorporating change suits each?
a: Pricing factors: configuration, or end-user customisation by the actuaries, because the change is frequent and each code change would be expensive. Layout: a code change is fine, because it is rare and the development cost of making it customisable would not pay back. Invest in cheap change where change is likely.

q: A requirements document says 'the system shall support other payment methods in future' and 'reporting: to be decided in phase 2'. What does this tell the architect?
a: These are open-ended and deferred requirements, which signal a high likelihood of change. Put variation points there: a payment-method interface, and reporting fed from well-defined data. Spending the same effort on areas with stable requirements would be wasted.

q: A B2B SaaS product has five enterprise clients, each with a dedicated implementation team, and each wants its own approval rules. Which change mechanism fits?
a: Customisable by the implementation team: build configurable rules or workflows that each client's team sets up. Development cost is high, but each change is medium-cost and needs no core code change. Full end-user customisation would cost even more to build and isn't needed when trained implementers do the changes.

q: A team wants to add a fraud-analytics consumer to the existing OrderPlaced events, but the event does not carry the customer's IP address, which the model needs. Is this still a change-free extension?
a: No. A new consumer avoids producer changes only when the existing payload already meets its needs. Here the producer must add the field, ideally as an optional addition registered as a compatible new schema version, so existing consumers keep working. Events still couple consumers to the payload's content and meaning.

q: Five microservices read and write one shared customer table, and renaming a column needs a coordinated release of all five. What has gone wrong?
a: Shared data has coupled the services, defeating independent deployment. Give the customer data a single owning service and have the others use its API or events. If that split is not worth it, a modular monolith may contain changes just as well at lower operational cost.

q: A producer renames the field 'amount' to 'total' and registers the change as version 2 in the schema registry. Are consumers safe?
a: No. The registry stores versioned schemas and lets consumers find the one a message uses, but an incompatible change still breaks consumers that expect 'amount'. Add 'total' alongside 'amount', migrate the consumers, and only then remove the old field, following compatibility rules.

q: In a layered monolith, adding a 'gift card' feature touches the presentation, business and persistence layers. Would a modular monolith help?
a: Yes, for this kind of change. A modular monolith groups code by business module, so a gift-card module contains its own UI, logic and data access, and the change stays inside it. It still deploys as one unit, so you don't get independent deployment; that would need services.

q: A public API method has 7 parameters, and clients keep breaking whenever a parameter is added. What would you change?
a: Pass a single request object, so new optional fields can be added without changing the method signature. Old clients must still be served correctly: keep existing fields and meanings, give new fields defaults, and test existing consumers. Version the API for changes that cannot be compatible.

q: A bank receives statements from 12 partners in CSV, XML and fixed-width formats, and parsing logic is spread across the system. What would you change?
a: Separate physical from logical processing: convert each physical format into one standard logical structure at the edge, and use only that structure in the rest of the system. A new partner format then changes only a converter. The cost is one more mapping layer to maintain.

q: A discount rate of 0.15 is hard-coded in 9 places, and the last change missed one. Which tactic would have prevented this?
a: Single point of definition: define the rate once, in configuration or a constant used everywhere, so a change never has to be synchronised across copies. Parameterising it in configuration also lets you change it without a code release.

q: A JSON API adds a mandatory field to every request. Is it backward compatible because the method signature is unchanged?
a: No. Existing callers omit the new field and may fail validation. Add it as optional with suitable behaviour for old callers, or version the breaking contract and migrate consumers.

q: Each of 30 corporate clients wants a different expense-approval chain, and the chains change a few times a year. How would you design it?
a: Defer binding with a workflow engine: an implementer designs each client's workflow, it is stored per tenant, and at run time the engine loads and executes it, calling shared domain logic. Changes need no recompiling or redeployment. The cost is building or adopting the engine and limiting workflows to the steps it supports.

q: For a 3-month MVP, a team proposes fully end-user-customisable reports. Do you agree?
a: Probably not. End-user customisation has the lowest change cost when done well, but the highest development cost, and it needs strong UX and domain understanding that an MVP rarely has. Ship a few fixed reports, learn which variations users actually want, and add customisation where that demand is clear.

q: A checkout error appears in the logs of four services, but nothing links the entries. What would you add?
a: A correlation id created at the entry point and passed with every call and event, and written in each service's log entries. Then the entries for one request can be pulled together for root-cause analysis. Central log storage alone does not show which records belong together.

q: Container logs disappear when pods restart, and engineers SSH into nodes to grep for errors. What would you change?
a: Add the three logging components: an agent on each node that ships logs, central log storage, and a dashboard with search (EFK is the lecture's example stack). Logs then survive restarts and can be searched across services. The cost is running and sizing the logging infrastructure itself.

q: A legacy application crashes every night and leaves nothing useful behind. Which analyzability tactics apply?
a: Automated error detection and reporting (core dumps, log file monitoring that raises alerts), logging with enough context to investigate, and monitoring through standard protocols such as JMX or SNMP. Together these turn 'it crashed' into a diagnosable fault.

q: The architecture rule says the web layer must not call the persistence layer directly. Code reviews keep missing violations. What would you add?
a: A fitness function: an automated test using a dependency-analysis tool that fails the build when web code depends on persistence packages. It checks the rule on every build, which review cannot do reliably. It guards only the rules you actually encode, so add checks for other key characteristics as well.

q: A release breaks checkout, and reverting takes 3 hours because the database migrations cannot be undone. What should the release process have included?
a: Rollback designed in: reversible or backward-compatible migrations, and the ability to redeploy the previous version quickly. Even tested changes fail in production, and fast reversal limits the damage. Version control, automated tests and environment configuration as code make that reversal reliable.

q: A release works in staging but fails in production, because the two environments were configured by hand and differ. A developer suggests committing the production passwords into the repository so everything is in one place. Respond.
a: Manage environment configuration as code, so staging and production are built from the same versioned definitions. Do not commit secret values: integrate a secrets-management tool, and reference secrets from the configuration. Reproducible environments without leaked credentials make change reliable.

q: A quality dashboard improves after a release. Does that prove the architecture is easier to maintain?
a: No. Check what changed in the metrics and whether they reflect relevant change or diagnostic effort. Combine trends with actual change scenarios and fitness checks; a score is evidence for its measured properties, not all maintainability.

q: A manager wants to rank three teams' systems by their static-analysis scores to decide bonuses. Do you agree?
a: No. These metrics are useful for tracking one code base's relative progress over time, not for comparing different systems in absolute terms, since size, language and domain differ. Using them for bonuses also invites gaming. Compare each team against its own trend, alongside real change effort.

q: A product's discount and eligibility rules change every quarter, and three of its 20 enterprise clients need their own approval flow. The business wants changes shipped without redeployment. Recommend a design and its costs.
a: Defer binding for the kinds of change that recur: hold rule parameters in configuration, which business users edit through an admin screen, behind a single point of definition. Use a workflow engine to run per-tenant approval flows designed by the implementation team. Encapsulate the domain actions the workflows call, and define the supported variation points. This lowers the cost of each change but raises development cost, and needs UX and domain work. Behaviour outside the variation points still needs a code change, so choose the variation points from the expected changes.

q: An online learning platform has a layered monolith, five teams and frequent collisions between releases. It plans to add analytics, recommendations and partner integrations over two years. Compare a modular monolith, microservices and an event-driven approach for modifiability, and recommend one.
a: Modular monolith: business modules contain changes and avoid distributed costs, but everything still deploys as one unit, so release collisions remain. Microservices: independent deployment per capability if each owns its data and APIs evolve compatibly, but they add operational cost, and shared tables or call chains can still spread change. Event-driven: analytics and recommendations can subscribe to existing events (CourseCompleted, LessonViewed) without producer changes if the payloads carry what they need, with a schema registry and compatibility rules. Recommend modularising first, then extracting services where team collisions are worst, and publishing events for the new consumers.

q: A public REST API has about 200 external consumers you do not control. Over the next year you must add fields, rename one concept and change one response structure. Which code-level tactics keep the API evolvable?
a: Use request and response objects with optional fields, so additions don't break signatures. Add the renamed concept alongside the old one and deprecate the old name with a support period. Put the structural change in a new API version, keeping the old one running during migration. Encapsulate the implementation behind the API, define the shared data types once, and use standard formats. Test existing consumer contracts, because flexible JSON syntax alone does not guarantee compatibility.

q: During an incident, a payment fails somewhere across six microservices. It takes four hours to find the cause because logs are local to each container and have no common identifier. Redesign for analyzability.
a: Add automated error detection and alerting, so the failure is noticed rather than reported by users. Centralise logs with an agent, storage and searchable dashboard (for example EFK), so they survive container restarts. Propagate a correlation id from the entry point through every call and event, so one request's entries can be retrieved together. Log enough context, such as inputs, the dependency called and the error, and expose metrics through standard monitoring. The fix itself is then deployed like any other change, through the reliable-change pipeline.

q: A layered system's dependency rules are eroding, releases often break production, and rollbacks are manual. Design a pipeline that makes change reliable and stops further erosion.
a: Keep everything in version control, including environment configuration as code, with secrets in a secrets manager. Run automated unit, integration and end-to-end tests on each change. Add fitness functions before promotion: a dependency test that fails on layer violations, plus performance, security, resiliency and observability checks. Automate deployment with a tested rollback path and reversible migrations, and use hypothesis-driven testing for risky changes. Fitness functions guard only what they encode, so add rules as the architecture evolves.

q: A city's parking-permit system receives about 30,000 applications in the first week of each year and about 200 a week afterwards. It must take a nightly file from the vehicle registry, and two developers will maintain it. Stakeholders propose microservices. Do you agree? Which qualities and styles should drive the choice?
a: Probably not microservices. With two developers and one product, the operational cost (discovery, gateways, automation) outweighs independent deployment. The driving qualities are elasticity for the January spike and cost the rest of the year, plus reliable file-level integration with the registry. A modular tiered application on an elastic platform, with file-level data flow for the registry feed, meets them more simply. Record the qualities as measurable scenarios in a utility tree, so the choice can be revisited if more teams or functions arrive.

q: A ticket-resale marketplace runs in two regions. Buyers browse listings, sellers update prices, and a purchase must never sell the same ticket twice. Which operations favour availability during a partition, which messaging style suits notifying sellers, and which views would you give operations and auditors?
a: Browsing listings and showing prices can favour availability with short staleness. The purchase must favour consistency, waiting or rejecting during a partition, because selling a ticket twice is unacceptable, and an ACID label does not settle partition behaviour. Notify sellers by publish/subscribe, so email, push and analytics subscribe independently. Give operations the physical and deployment views (regions, nodes, failover) and auditors the information-structure and deployment views showing where payment data lives and who can reach it.

q: A physical diagram already names products and server sizes, but the team has not agreed the business rules or the peak load. How would you get the architecture process back on track?
a: Go back to Define Requirements: stakeholders including technical ones, a glossary, a system context, then functional requirements and NFRs with measurable targets and conditions. Prioritise the architecturally significant ones. Derive the logical architecture (boundary, control and entity components, logical nodes) and verify it. Only then map it to technology and size the nodes against the NFRs, keeping the existing product choices as recorded decisions with alternatives and assumptions, so they can be overturned if the requirements contradict them.

q: IROne-style requirements: search 99.9% available within 3 s, other functions 99% within 5 s, 1000 concurrent users, and integration with hotel systems reachable only through messaging. A benchmark shows one application node handles 300 users at target. Outline the logical-to-physical decisions you would record.
a: Map search one to many: capacity needs 1000 / 300, about 3.3, so 4 nodes; to survive one failure, 5 (4 survivors x 300 = 1,200). Other functions can share fewer nodes if they are isolated from search. Map the hotel boundaries to messaging, and flag the transformation in the endpoint table as adapter work to specify and test. Record each choice in the Issue, Decision, Assumptions, Alternatives, Justification format, especially the 300-user figure, and validate it with a proof of concept under the real request mix.

q: A system uses TLS, but an administrator account exports confidential records with no business need. Trace the risk and propose two different kinds of control.
a: Asset: the confidential records; threat: misuse of privileged access; vulnerability: excessive permissions and no monitoring. Assess likelihood and impact, then treat. Apply least privilege and role-based access (technical, preventive), and audit logging with alerts on bulk exports (technical, detective), backed by regular access reviews (administrative, detective). TLS protects data in transit; it does not decide who should read the records.

q: A telehealth service runs video consultations and stores consultation notes. TLS terminates at a load balancer in the DMZ, clinicians log in with a password, and a vendor supports the video servers remotely. Identify the top three risks and choose a control for each, stating its type and category.
a: First, stolen clinician passwords give access to patient notes (spoofing, authenticity). Control: MFA (technical, preventive). Second, plaintext at the DMZ load balancer exposes notes if it is compromised (information disclosure). Control: encrypt the notes for the back end, or terminate TLS deeper, and harden the load balancer (technical, preventive). Third, the vendor's remote access becomes a stepping stone. Control: an MFA-protected, logged jump host on a segregated admin network (technical, preventive and detective). Add IDS and log review so the design is not only preventive, and record the residual risk.

q: Two app servers replace one, but the database and network remain shared. Peak-time latency still fails its target. What should you inspect before adding a third?
a: Measure response time, queueing, throughput and per-resource utilisation to find the real bottleneck: if the shared database is saturated, a third app server adds load to it without adding throughput. Map required dependencies and shared failure points too, because two app servers do nothing for a database or network failure. Add app servers only if that tier is the limit; otherwise scale or offload the database (caching, read replicas, fewer visits per request).

q: Two app servers in parallel, 99% available each, run at 70% CPU during peak. A teammate claims the tier is now 99.99% available. Do you agree?
a: Not at peak. The 99.99% figure assumes either server can carry the full load alone, but if one fails, the survivor would need 140% of its capacity, so it saturates, queues grow without bound and the service is effectively down. Either size so that one server can carry the peak (each below about 50% at peak, preferably lower to keep response times acceptable) or add a third server. Then the parallel calculation is justified, provided failover works and failures are independent.

q: Search works from cache during a database outage, but checkout fails. Is the system available?
a: Judge each function against its own requirement: cached search is available, and checkout is not. If the agreed service counts checkout as critical, the service is unavailable for that purpose, whatever the search page shows. A circuit breaker and cache provide graceful degradation, but checkout availability needs a redundant data tier or a degraded mode, such as holding orders for later confirmation, if the business accepts it.

q: The disk may fill in eight weeks, procurement takes seven, and moving to a new store also risks breaking clients. How would you combine capacity planning and maintainability?
a: Validate the forecast first: compare linear and exponential fits and include logs and indexes, because the earlier date may already be inside the lead time. Start procurement or interim capacity now, with a buffer. Protect clients by putting storage behind a stable interface, using compatibility checks and staging the migration with a rollback path. Use monitoring and fitness checks to confirm capacity and catch failures after the change.

q: Forecast peak demand is 80 requests/s, and each node sustainably handles 35 requests/s. How many nodes do you need to survive the loss of one node, and what would make that number wrong?
a: Four: three survivors give 105 requests/s, while two would give only 70. The number is wrong if the 35 requests/s came from a benchmark with a different request mix, if scaling is sub-linear (shared data or crosstalk, per Amdahl and USL), or if a shared dependency such as the database saturates first. Verify with a load test at the production mix, and test failover.

q: A SaaS product's pricing rules change monthly, and its tenant count doubles every year. A teammate proposes per-tenant code branches to handle client-specific rules. Respond, covering both maintainability and capacity.
a: Reject per-tenant branches: every fix must be repeated across branches, and the cost of change grows with every tenant. Use deferred binding instead, with per-tenant configuration or workflows loaded at run time behind defined variation points. For capacity, the doubling tenant count drives both cumulative storage and peak server load, so forecast both from tenant growth, using application metrics such as tenants and requests per tenant. Check the scaling with load tests, since a configuration lookup on every request adds work.

q: A resort reservation system must take 1,500 concurrent bookings at the 8 am release of holiday slots, survive the loss of any one server, and let the business change its booking rules every quarter without a release. How would you turn these goals into a defensible architecture, and what evidence would you need before committing?
a: Write each goal as a measurable scenario (for example, '90% of bookings confirmed within 3 s with 1,500 concurrent users at 8 am') and rank them in a utility tree. Derive boundary, control and entity components, then map the booking control one to many across nodes sized so the survivors still carry the peak. Put the rules behind a configuration or rules-engine variation point, and record that decision with its assumptions. Before committing, benchmark the booking scenario with the real request mix, calculate end-to-end availability including shared dependencies, and test failover. Benchmarks rarely scale linearly, and a topology label proves nothing.

q: Two million smart meters each send a reading every 15 minutes, and most send in the first minute of each window. The current design writes every reading synchronously into one primary database with one read replica, and it is falling behind. Propose a plan to scale the writes and name two side effects to monitor.
a: The average is about 2,200 writes/s, but the real peak is about 33,000/s if most of the 2 million arrive within 60 s, and that is what to size for. Put a durable queue or event stream in front of the database, so ingestion absorbs the burst and writers drain it at a sustainable rate. Then partition (shard) the readings by meter id across several primaries, since a read replica adds no write capacity, and batch the inserts. Side effects to monitor: queue lag, meaning how stale the latest reading is, against any freshness requirement; and uneven shards or hot partitions. Cross-shard queries and reports also become harder, so feed them from the stream or a separate analytics store.

q: A teammate proposes 'number of monthly active users' as the metric showing that a booking platform is scalable and highly available. Do you agree? What would you measure instead?
a: No. Monthly active users measures adoption volume, not how the system behaves as load grows or how often it is unavailable. A high count says nothing about response time at peak, and could rise while users suffer outages. For scalability, measure throughput and response-time percentiles against load (for example p90 response at 1x, 2x and 4x peak) and how throughput grows as nodes are added. For availability, measure (agreed service time - downtime) / agreed service time per critical function, plus MTTR.

q: A logical packaging and deployment model puts the web front end, booking service and payment adapter in one deployable on a single node in the DMZ, with the database on the same node. Identify the undesirable decisions and propose corrective actions.
a: First, everything sits in the DMZ: compromising the web front end exposes the booking logic, payment adapter and data. Keep only the web tier or reverse proxy in the DMZ, and place the services and database behind an inner firewall with only the required traffic allowed. Second, one node and one deployable is a single point of failure that cannot scale by tier. Separate the deployables, run the booking service one to many behind a load balancer, and give the database its own redundant nodes. Third, the payment adapter is bundled with unrelated code, so a payment change forces a full redeploy. Make it its own unit behind a stable interface. Each correction adds nodes and operating cost, which must be justified against the availability, security and modifiability scenarios.
